Sports.title: UEFA president 'boycotts' World Cup final after Donald Trump and FIFA outrage
Sports.content:
UEFA president 'boycotts' World Cup final after Donald Trump and FIFA outrage

UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin was not at the World Cup final between Spain and Argentina

View 2 Images UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin (R) was not at the World Cup final due to a reported breakdown in relationship with FIFA. (Image: Getty Images)

UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin reportedly boycotted the World Cup final between Spain and Argentina 'in protest' against FIFA after a breakdown in relations between the two governing bodies. Ceferin, who also serves as FIFA vice-president, was notably absent from the showpiece finale yesterday.

‌



While Donald Trump and several other high profile figures attended the game, Ceferin was nowhere to be seen. The Times claims the Slovenian's absence was a result of the Folarin Balogun saga, which saw FIFA suspend a red card offence for the United States striker after he was sent off, meaning he was eligible to play against Belgium.

‌



UEFA released a damning statement in the aftermath of FIFA's decision, which read: "Yesterday’s decision to suspend for a probationary period of a year the implementation of the one-match automatic suspension following the red card issued to the player Folarin Balogun crossed a red line.

‌



UEFA's five major issues with FIFA World Cup as president snub highlights divide READ MORE :

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

"Football, like any other sports, relies on rules, which are the basis for fair, honest and transparent competition. Sometimes rules are open to interpretation. In this case not. A minimum automatic suspension of one match following a red card is not a discretionary option and does not require the decision of a competent body to be enacted.

"It is a principle embedded in regulations, which cannot be made subject to exceptions, let alone in the middle of a tournament where several other players have been in the same situation and regularly served their suspension.

‌



"When the certainty of rules is no longer guaranteed by its guardians, the integrity of the game is at stake and the credibility of a competition is undermined. Equally, such decision creates a precedent in the ongoing tournament, where similar situations will now require an equal treatment, to the detriment of the competition.

"Football is the most loved sport in the world because it is a beautiful game and is trusted because it is played everywhere with the same laws.

"A tournament is never a pure standalone and, if the tournament in question is the World Cup, it has the power to drive positive or negative consequences on the game as a whole. We express our disbelief at such an unprecedented, incomprehensible and unjustifiable decision."

‌



View 2 Images UEFA president Alexander Ceferin and FIFA boss Gianni Infantino (Image: Masashi Hara, Getty Images)

It's not the only major decision that FIFA have made in recent months to upset the UEFA chief. Those include the proposed expansion of the World Cup to 64 teams, half-time shows and high ticket prices for the tournament.

There was also a debacle surrounding Somalian referee Omar Artan, who was denied entry to the US before the tournament started. After that decision, UEFA installed him as the official as referee for the Super Cup match between PSG and Aston Villa later this summer.

Article continues below

There have also been murmurings throughout the summer that UEFA could pitch a candidate to run against Gianni Infantino at the next FIFA presidential election, with the Italian previously thought to be running unopposed.

The current FIFA head-honcho has outlined his intention to run for a third campaign, but there is growing support for other candidates within UEFA.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi shows true colours with emotional message after World Cup final loss
Sports.content:
Lionel Messi shows true colours with emotional message after World Cup final loss

Argentina came up short in their bid to win back-to-back World Cups and their captain and talisman Lionel Messi has broken his silence following the defeat to Spain

View 2 Images Lionel Messi has spoken after Argentina's World Cup final loss (Image: FIFA via Getty Images)

Lionel Messi has penned an open letter to Argentina supporters following their unsuccessful bid to become just the third team in history to win successive World Cups.

‌



Messi and Co went into Sunday's final with Spain as the defending champions after victory in Qatar back in 2022. But Argentina were very much second best against Luis de la Fuente's side, who dominated from start to finish. Ferran Torres plundered the only goal of the game in extra-time after Enzo Fernandez had been sent off for a moment of madness in the final minutes of regulation time.

‌



At 39 years of age, there is every chance Sunday's final in New Jersey was Messi's final World Cup appearance.

‌



The eight-time Ballon d'Or winner broke down after the game when he was serenaded by Argentina fans. Nearly 24 hours later, he has taken to social media to speak about the pain of said defeat, while also congratulating Spain on their win.

World Cup final LIVE: FIFA investigation launched after disgraceful Argentina throw punches at Spain stars READ MORE :

UEFA's five major issues with FIFA World Cup as president snub highlights divide READ MORE :

“The pain is immense, it will take time for this wound to heal. But I also choose to hold on to all the good things, all matches we turned around by giving everything and moments that will remain in our memories forever.

“I will always remember the support of an entire country that, together with the work and effort of this group, brought us back once again among the best teams in the world.

‌



“Today, it is difficult to appreciate what we achieved… but this group has really reached two consecutive World Cup finals. Thank you from the bottom of my heart for every greeting and every message. Once again, we managed to come together as a country and stand united, sharing the immense pride of being Argentine.

View 2 Images Messi was devastated after the final whistle (Image: FIFA via Getty Images)

“I also want to congratulate Spain on winning World Cup.”

‌



The aftermath of the World Cup final was marred by ugly scenes as Nahuel Molina and Leandro Paredes both lashed out at opponents.

Wayne Rooney condemned their actions, saying: “Does it surprise you? It doesn't surprise me. We've seen this with Argentina before.

“It's just not the reaction you want. We've seen some of the reaction after knocking England out in the last round. That's just sad. If you lose a game of football, be graceful and get out of there. It's really poor from them.”

Sports.title: Menzies shocks world No 2 Humphries in World Matchplay thriller
Sports.content:
Cameron Menzies produced a massive upset to defeat 2024 champion Luke Humphries 10-7 at the World Matchplay on Monday night.

World No 2 Humphries took centre stage against one of the most entertaining and unpredictable players in the game in Menzies.

And it was the Scot who raised the Empress Ballroom roof with an inspired 170 checkout to stun the former world champion and seal his first win on the Winter Gardens stage.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Cameron Menzies lands 'The Big Fish' to stun Luke Humphries at the World Matchplay

Betfred World Matchplay - Monday's results

Round Two

Ross Smith 10-6 Kevin Doets Gerwyn Price 11-9 Martin Schindler Cameron Menzies 10-7 Luke Humphries Rob Cross 10-3 Danny Noppert

Menzies produced a brilliant double-double 129 finish to lead Humphries 3-2, but 'Cool Hand' made it six consecutive breaks of throw with a magnificent 167 checkout to level straight after the first interval.

Menzies then went on a blistering four-leg burst to race into a 7-3 lead but could only win one out of the next five legs as Humphries went on a charge.

However, Menzies landed an inspired 170 checkout to cause a mighty shock as he set up a second-round clash with Ross Smith.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Humphries pinned this stunning 167 on the bull

"No one gave me hope! I didn't give myself hope but I finally won a game at the Winter Gardens," said a delighted Menzies.

"Luke Humphries is a great guy, a great player. At 7-3 I was just trying not to think of that finishing line but the nerves kicked in. To beat Humphries, I know he will be disappointed. He gave me a lot of stress at doubles but that's my biggest win.

"I show a lot of emotion and I hate that I do that. I'm trying to keep myself intact. Try to keep myself composed because I know he was going to have a spell and batter me and he had a little spell but lucky enough I had that lead.

"I know that's not Humphries but I'll take it any day of the week."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Menzies hits this HUGE double-double finish against Humphries

Mardle: Menzies' greatest moment - he knows he can handle anything now

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Hear from Menzies and Wayne Mardle after the Scotsman claimed a famous win over Humphries

"It's his best ever win, and he mentioned that," said Wayne Mardle, speaking to Sky Sports.

"With Cameron Menzies, everyone mentions his emotions, but it's the way he had to win that game.

"Nothing went according to plan. He was broken back early twice, that's up-and-down emotions. The high of breaking to being broken back.

"Then he went on a run, and got pegged back. There was a lot happening in that game, but he held it all together beautifully.

"Humphries had an amazing spell of four legs, but then Menzies found a level again, and that's something we don't see enough.

"What he should take away from tonight was the way he handled this situation. It was like he was there a million times before.

"He knows he can handle anything now."

Humphries vs Menzies: Tale of the Tape

Menzies to face 'Smudger' next

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player It was very nearly a debut to forget for Kevin Doets as he came close to taking a tumble on the stage

Ross Smith came through a fantastic encounter as he defied a 104.19 average from debutant Kevin Doets - taking out 160 and a match-winning 120 - to reach the second round.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Doets hiit this 161 finish on the bullseye - just in time to save the match!

'Hawkeye' saved the match with a stunning 161 checkout but Smith held the Dutchman at arm's length.

After storming out of the gates to a 5-0 lead 'Smudger' kept his composure through a mid-session scrap before sealing victory - signing off with a spectacular 120 Shanghai finish.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Smith nailed this magnificent 160 checkout on his way to victory

Price wins in extra time to set up Cross showdown

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gerwyn Price nails the ton checkout to sink Martin Schindler

Former World Matchplay finalist Gerwyn Price survived a huge scare against German No 1 Martin Schindler to book his spot in the second round.

'The Iceman' trailed 4-0 and 6-2 before roaring back and punishing Schindler for errors on the outer ring to win 11-9.

"It doesn't usually happen. Without the crowd, I would have lost today," admitted Price. "That was the worst I've played all season.

"It goes to show, throwing sheep about instead of darts about, it doesn't help! It was a tough one for me. I've got no confidence at the minute because I haven't played a lot.

"To battle through it. Martin was just as rubbish as me, thankfully.

"That was one I should have lost, but I've won and I'm still in the tournament - I can't be any worse!"

Price will take on Rob Cross next after 'Voltage' kicked off his campaign with a convincing 10-3 win over Danny Noppert.

The 2019 champion led 5-0 at the break and never relented, averaging 97.41, pinning a 128 checkout, and ending with an impressive 52.6 per cent on the doubles.

What's happening at the World Matchplay on Tuesday?

Image: Luke Littler and Michael van Gerwen headline the World Matchplay action on Tuesday

The 2026 Betfred World Matchplay continues at the iconic Winter Gardens from July 18-26, as a 32-player field compete for the prestigious Phil Taylor Trophy.

Two-time world champion Luke Littler takes on Nathan Aspinall in a blockbuster clash after opening his defence of the Phil Taylor Trophy with a sensational 10-6 win over Niko Springer on Day One in Blackpool.

Betfred World Matchplay - Tuesday's fixtures [first to 11 legs]

Round Two - Evening 7pm

Jonny Clayton vs Gary Anderson Michael van Gerwen vs Dirk van Duijvenbode Luke Littler vs Nathan Aspinall Josh Rock vs Stephen Bunting

Stephen Bunting takes on Josh Rock after winning through a Winter Gardens classic against debutant Niels Zonneveld, surviving three match darts to edge past the Dutchman 13-12.

Three-time World Matchplay winner Michael van Gerwen faces fellow Dutchman Dirk van Duijvenbode, while Gary Anderson - the 2018 champion - goes up against 2023 runner-up Jonny Clayton having recorded the eighth-highest average in World Matchplay history, averaging 109.96 in his 10-2 demolition of Ryan Joyce.

Sports.title: Palace seek £55m-plus for Lacroix as talks with Chelsea begin
Sports.content:
Chelsea are in talks with Crystal Palace over the signing of defender Maxence Lacroix.

Sky Sports News understands Palace are seeking more than the £55m Tottenham paid for Jan Paul van Hecke from Brighton to sanction Lacroix's sale.

Palace and Chelsea enjoy good relations at the highest levels and they have done deals for players such as Trevoh Chalobah and Ben Chilwell.

Chelsea want to sign a centre-back and ideally any new arrival would be physically imposing and bring Premier League experience.

Chelsea have raised around £130m from sales in this window and more players are set to leave.

In defence, players who could move on include Chalobah, Benoit Badiashile, Malo Gusto and Axel Disasi.

Rogers arrives for medical ahead of record-breaking move

Morgan Rogers arrived for a medical with Chelsea on Monday morning, which you can exclusively watch below, ahead of completing a British-record £117m move from Aston Villa.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Morgan Rogers has been spotted arriving for his Chelsea medical after the Blues agreed a £117m deal with Aston Villa.

All being well, Rogers is then expected to sign a six-year contract at Chelsea with the option of another year until 2033.

Rogers returned from the USA on Sunday following England's third-place finish at the World Cup, via a bronze-final victory over France.

Chelsea moved quickly to secure the deal ahead of Arsenal, who were unwilling to match the asking price despite Rogers being their top forward target.

Image: Morgan Rogers will become Chelsea's most expensive player

Rogers will become the most expensive British player of all time when he completes his move from Aston Villa, with the fee eclipsing the £116m fee paid by Manchester City for his England team-mate Elliot Anderson.

Rogers is also set to become Chelsea's record signing, overtaking the £115m the Blues paid Brighton for Moises Caicedo in 2023.

Sports.title: Brundle: The Hamilton-Russell penalty call and Antonelli's class of one
Sports.content:
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Belgian Grand Prix.

The Kimi Antonelli show, also known as the 2026 Belgian Grand Prix, took place in remarkably sunny and dry conditions throughout, if occasionally interrupted by an actual safety car deployment on lap one to clear a beached car, and a few more virtual safety cars to clear up high-tech litter from the racing surface.

The Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps has been developed and polished beautifully in almost every respect, even if in time-honoured fashion getting into and moving around the venue seems to have new systems and rules every day. To be fair, there is a huge area and a great many fans to be controlled.

As usual I was out and about trackside on Friday during practice and the cars looked very fast and impressive in front of the numerous grandstands. I've been racing here for 45 years, and I couldn't quite believe my eyes on the scale of the crowd.

It was enjoyable to watch the drivers jockey an excess of power over grip through medium-speed chicane exits, but like Silverstone there was a hidden story alongside the trackside 'wow', and the drivers were very restrained through the event not to complain too much about it.

We long ago lost Eau Rouge and Raidillon as corners to refined high-downforce cars with grippy tyres and a manicured racetrack, meaning from the turn one La Source hairpin to the long haul up to the turn five Les Combes chicane is effectively a straight.

Image: Kimi Antonelli rounds La Source during the race

But with the need to charge the hybrid batteries on this fast track, the longest on the calendar, just as with Copse, Becketts, and Stowe at Silverstone, as the engine is used to charge those batteries the arrival speeds into corners like Pouhon at Spa are dulled such that the corner effectively becomes a bendy straight too.

On such circuits we have lost the driver-defining, and thrilling, high-speed corners. It was the same in Suzuka.

Luckily in Budapest this weekend it will not be a problem at all, and normal service will be resumed, although there are no high-speed corners worth their name.

We have known for a while about these issues, and they are being addressed where possible for 2027 and again in 2028, but the last two races have unequivocally confirmed that we need a major power unit philosophy change much sooner than later.

There were always going to be teething problems reliability-wise but as we hurtle towards the summer break the words 'deployment issues' and 'no battery' are rather too prominent.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports F1's Martin Brundle takes you behind the scenes to show you how he prepares for his iconic Sunday 'Grid Walk'!

Russell's Mercedes problems and the 'racing incident' debate

George Russell is clearly not a direct descendant of the Alessandro Volta, Michael Faraday, Thomas Edison or Nikola Tesla families because he never seems to have the right battery power at the moment.

Whether that is missing straight-line speed compared to his team-mate Antonelli in qualifying, for whatever mystery reasons, or climbing the hill to turn five on the opening lap.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Drama at the start of the Belgium GP as George Russell's title hopes take a huge blow.

Antonelli got away well at the start and Verstappen's Red Bull launched unusually nicely too. But Max appeared to pull a cunning move by powering past before Eau Rouge at the bottom of the hill, but his post-race comments say that his car had too much battery deployment suggesting he had nothing to do with that cunning plan…

Both Mercedes of Antonelli and Russell started the race with less battery charge than needed, and it particularly hurt Russell on the long climb to the critical turn five braking point, and he was mugged by three cars including Lewis Hamilton.

George braked impressively late trying to make up for his poor arrival speed and was on the outside of Lewis, leaving racing room. Lewis, close behind Max, slid a little wide and contacted George who spun into retirement, and at the same time taking a massive hit to his championship comeback chances.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes driver George Russell spins after contact with Lewis Hamilton and his race ends on the opening lap, but was the Ferrari driver's penalty fair?

More referee leeway is given on the first lap with the pack inevitably in close company along with full fuel and sub-optimal brake and tyre temperatures. I called it a racing incident in commentary, unless the stewards were satisfied that Lewis had lost control of his car, which didn't appear to be the case.

George recovered to the pits by scooter and called it a racing incident whilst far more distraught about his ongoing power issues.

Ferrari called it a racing incident, I guess you could say they would, and most people I know agreed. But with whatever extra information the stewards had they applied a five-second penalty mitigated down from the standard 10 seconds. It perhaps cost Lewis a podium but that's speculative.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Oscar Piastri takes to his McLaren team radio to complain about contact with Ferrari's Charles Leclerc.

Later in the race, Charles Leclerc would squeeze Oscar Piastri in the T5 braking zone and there was contact which damaged Piastri's aero parts, to an extent. For me this was a clear movement in the braking zone which can mean anything from a warning flag to a full pit-lane drive through penalty in the guidelines.

The stewards, though, decided it was about relative front axle positions and who had the right to the corner. Leclerc's telling reaction when it was played out in the cooldown room tells us everything we need to know on that one.

The pit stops that did - and didn't - make the difference

Hamilton had a torrid weekend with an accident in practice, the five-second penalty with Russell, and nearly running one of his mechanics over in the pit stop through no fault of his own. That incident attracted a team fine rather than a race penalty and so Lewis was perhaps relieved to finish fourth, probably for the first time in his life.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The Ferrari pit crew were unable to tweak Lewis Hamilton's front wing level as the British driver knocked over a mechanic after being given the green light.

Piastri drove a spirited race to fifth despite his car damage although he lacked the same pace, which threatened to make the podium early on, after he swapped onto the hard compound tyres on lap 20 of 44.

Lando Norris drove beautifully all weekend but had to start 13th due to needing power unit control electronics beyond the allowance in the regulations, which is designed to keep costs down so that wealthy teams can't just throw new parts at the car every weekend.

Curiously McLaren chose not to use the virtual safety cars, or indeed a straightforward pit stop, until Lando eventually pitted on lap 30 to get rid of his starting hard-compound tyres. This left him with too much to do to catch Isack Hadjar who started his Red Bull from the back row of the grid, also due to numerous power unit penalties, to finish an impressive sixth.

Red Bull pitted Hadjar on lap one, and then again on lap two to cycle through the mandatory use of two different tyre compounds under cover of the Russell safety car, and then again under a virtual safety car on lap 20. Nicely done.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes Kimi Antonelli discusses his Belgian GP win and admits he's in a 'good position' after opening up a 45-point gap in the drivers' standings.

That same lap 20 VSC played out beautifully for Leclerc in his Ferrari as the time loss is only around 11 seconds when your rivals are lapping at reduced speed. Antonelli had pitted on lap 18 under full green conditions as Mercedes were covering off Red Bull's pit stop for Verstappen on lap 17.

Through all this Leclerc leapfrogged the pair of them and was now effectively leading, albeit with the yet-to-stop Norris ahead of him. Antonelli would hunt him down but perhaps not as rapidly as expected, Leclerc was driving beautifully.

'What a difference a year makes'

Eventually, and frankly inevitably given his speed throughout the event, the Italian teenager would take the lead, but Leclerc still wouldn't give up, and he finished second just two seconds adrift.

Verstappen would finish a solid third, Leclerc's safety car good fortune denied him a shot at second.

The final points went to Gabriel Bortoleto and Audi in eighth, Arvid Lindblad and Racing Bulls in ninth, and Franco Colapinto for Alpine in 10th. The safety cars played a role for and against throughout.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch from onboard Alpine's Franco Colapinto as he pulls off an incredible double overtake on Pierre Gasly and Liam Lawson at the Belgian GP.

What a difference a year makes. Antonelli never ran higher than 14th on his F1 debut here last year, but he was in a class of one this season.

Mercedes are on fire too, with their eighth victory of the season, which is one more than they won over the last four 'ground effect era' seasons combined. That combination will take some stopping from winning both championships in fine style.

Sports.title: A pioneer and a superstar, Kevin Keegan’s achievements were extraordinary
Sports.content:
Kevin Keegan, who has died aged 75, is the only British player to win the Ballon d’Or twice, was the star of Liverpool’s first European Cup-winning team, a messianic figure at Newcastle United as a player and coach, forging a team so memorable that Fifa’s president wrote to commend him, and was the captain and then manager of the England men’s national team. And yet, as Keegan would ruefully reflect, he will principally be remembered by many for an emotional outburst that precipitated Newcastle’s historic failure in a Premier League title race, a TV interview which presaged the coming era of the modern game.

Keegan’s “I’d love it” rant of April 1996, directed at Alex Ferguson, became a meme before the modern meaning of the word and social media even existed, repeatedly played on Sky Sports and becoming indelibly marked in the minds of multiple generations, many not even born when it occurred. It frequently tops polls as the most memorable moment in Premier League history and foreshadowed an era where digital clips and personality narratives would dominate football coverage.

There is a danger, however, of reducing Keegan’s life to a series of ever-more emotional explosions, of which there were many, such as his punch-up with Leeds United’s Billy Bremner in the 1974 Charity Shield. For that would obscure the extraordinary nature of his achievements and the fact he was arguably the most charismatic modern English footballer; more eloquent than David Beckham and Paul Gascoigne and more passionate than Bobby Moore. He had a rare gift for inspiring players and almost everyone who interacted with him at his best came away uplifted.

Still, Keegan’s meltdown on TV, where he took issue with Ferguson’s supposed “mind games” in suggesting Leeds players would go easy on Newcastle during a tight title run-in with Manchester United, became a defining moment. “Strangers shout ‘love it’ to me from car windows,” wrote Keegan in his autobiography. “Autograph hunters tell me they would ‘love it’ if I could sign their pieces of paper. When I go to charity events I am often asked to sign photographs showing me in that classic pose: headphones on, finger jabbing, blazing eyes. Those pictures tend to be auctioned for a lot more money than the ones where I am playing for England or any of my clubs.”

Keegan claimed to be relaxed about the characterisation, skewed though it was, perhaps because more than any English footballer before he had maximised football’s commercial and media opportunities and accepted the respective bouquets and brickbats that ensued. Even before that meltdown, he would be best remembered by many in the 1970s for his excruciating bike crash on Superstars, a TV show which pitted athletes from different sports against each other in unfamiliar disciplines. Sprawled across the cycle track, Keegan’s bare flesh was ripped red raw by the gravel. Most remember the drama but few recall that, showing characteristic pig-headed determination, he got back on the bike, bloodied and bandaged, for a rematch, which he won before winning the entire contest.

Keegan was born in Armthorpe, Doncaster, to Doris and Joe, a war veteran Durham miner who had migrated south in search of work at Markham colliery. His upbringing echoed Monty Python’s Yorkshiremen sketch, only his memories were authentic, a throwback to a different century. Their terrace house “had a detached outhouse where we washed. Our bath was an old zinc tub and the toilet was at the foot of the garden and we never had electricity until I was 10 and we moved into a council house in Balby.”

View image in fullscreen Kevin Keegan shares a joke with Alex Ferguson after the rollercoaster 1995-96 season. Photograph: Adam Butler/PA

Keegan’s ascent to the peak of the game’s elite was unforeseen, few recognising his talent early on, most dismissing him as too small. He always credited Sister Mary Oliver, the nun who ran his Catholic primary school football team and who refereed with a crucifix around her neck, as being as important to him as a mentor as Bill Shankly was. “Kevin’s football must be encouraged,” she wrote in a school report, which gave him immense self-belief.

Doncaster Rovers rejected him and he started work at Peglers Brass Works at 16, playing for their football team but only in the reserves and also for a pub team on Sundays, where he fortuitously played against a Scunthorpe scout, Bob Nellis, who got him a trial at the struggling Third Division club. Keegan referred to himself as a “mongrel” and “weasel” and the “least-talented” Ballon d’Or winner, and despite impressing at Scunthorpe it was still a major shock when Shankly, the man he regarded as a second father and progenitor of his success, took him to Liverpool. Shankly told him: “You’re not just a great player – you’re one of the great players!” It seemed an unlikely boast but Keegan scored on his Liverpool debut and was never dropped thereafter. He would inherit from Shankly comparable motivational skills.

Quick Guide The Keegan years: from player to manager Show 1951 Kevin Keegan is born on 14 February in Armthorpe, near Doncaster. 1968 Begins playing career at Scunthorpe United. 1971 Signed by Bill Shankly for Liverpool at age of 20, initially as a midfielder. 1972 Makes England debut against Wales in November. 1973 Liverpool win the league; Keegan scores twice in Uefa Cup final win over Borussia Mönchengladbach. 1974 Scores twice as Liverpool beat Newcastle 3-0 in the FA Cup final. His first England goal comes against Wales. 1976 Liverpool win the league title and Keegan scores in each leg of Uefa Cup final win against Club Brugge. His celebrity is such he appears on the TV show Superstars, and famously crashes his bike during one of the races. 1977 Another league title for Liverpool, who also win their first European Cup, a 3-1 victory over Mönchengladbach. Keegan moves to Hamburg for £500,000, nearly double the German transfer record. 1978 Wins Ballon d’Or. 1979 Wins Ballon d’Or again as Hamburg secure their first German ‌championship title in 19 years, and first in the Bundesliga era. 1980 Captains England at Euros but they are knocked out in the group stage. Leaves Hamburg to join Southampton for two seasons. 1982 Transfers to Newcastle in the Second Division. Plays final match for England, after 63 caps (31 as captain) and 21 goals. 1984 Helps Newcastle secure promotion in his second season, then retires from playing. Across his club career, he scores 204 goals in 592 ‌appearances. 1992 Takes first coaching role as manager of struggling Newcastle in February. Danger of relegation to the Third Division is averted. 1993 Leads them to the First Division title and promotion to the Premier League in his first full season in charge. 1994 Newcastle finish third in Premier League. 1996 Newcastle finish second in the Premier League, ​despite leading for most ​of campaign – by 12 points at one stage. Season includes famous “I would love it if we beat them” comments when discussing rivals Manchester United on Sky Sports. 1997 Leaves Newcastle and takes over at Fulham for two seasons. 1999 Takes charge ​of England national ‌team in February. 2000 Coaches England at Euro 2000 where they beat Germany but still go out in the group stage. Resigns in ​October after a 1–0 loss to Germany in World Cup qualifying. 2001 Takes over at Manchester City. 2008 Returns to Newcastle but lasts eight months after tensions with the board and owner Mike Ashley. Though reclusive, Keegan also had a streak of extrovertism, embracing every aspect of the game’s growing commercial opportunities, from his famous Brut advert to appearances on Top of the Pops, where his single Head Over Heels in Love reached the top 40. Though he enjoyed standing out, he admitted he would never have got away with his trademark bubble perm in the old-school Liverpool dressing room. His wife, Jean, whom he met on the waltzers at the Doncaster St Leger horse racing meeting when she was 16 and he was 19 and to whom he remained married for life, burst into fits of laughter when she first saw it. He had the last laugh, the hairstyle inspiring alarming copycat versions across the football world.

Keegan remained true to what he considered to be his working-class, mining roots, declaring himself a Labour man, annoyed that a staged photo of him feigning to kiss then prime minister Margaret Thatcher on the cheek was interpreted as support for economic policies which had ravaged heavy industry. He was more at home playing head tennis with a later PM, Tony Blair, to whom he was close enough to host at his home for dinner.

View image in fullscreen The then Newcastle manager Keegan chats to the Labour leader Tony Blair in the summer of 1996. Photograph: Adam Butler/PA

Keegan inherited two mantles from Britain’s greatest players of the 1960s. As George Best, the original footballer sex symbol of the modern era, lapsed into alcoholism and increasing unreliability, Keegan became the more wholesome and dependable commercial face of the superstar footballer in Britain, inundated with deals. For England he effectively became Moore’s successor as captain but at a time when the national team was in decline from his predecessor’s World Cup-winning heights. For Keegan, as the sole outfield world-class player, it was a heavy burden to bear as they missed out on successive World Cup finals.

His first major tournament for his country was the ill-fated 1980 European Championship and his World Cup career amounted to 20 minutes in 1982, a campaign which was disrupted by a back injury and where “my only contribution was a dreadful miss against the host nation to send us home. That moment is probably the only moment of my England career that people remember now.” It would prove to be his last game for England at the age of just 31.

More notable features of Keegan’s England career were his courage in defying IRA death threats to play against Northern Ireland in Belfast, then walking out on the team when Don Revie dropped him shortly afterwards and being arbitrarily beaten up by Yugoslav custom officials prior to a game in Belgrade, a horrific and wholly underserved ordeal that sparked an international incident. His frustration was best summed up in a story he told about the great Dutch player Johnny Rep. Surveying an England team at Wembley in 1977, Rep turned to Keegan and said: “Kevvy, you have problems here: this is the worst England side I have seen.” The Netherlands won 2-0 and, as Keegan recalled, could have scored at will.

Keegan was a pioneering player, negotiating release clauses, unheard of at the time in England, at Liverpool and Hamburg, allowing him to leave if a club met a £500,000 fee, thereby controlling his moves. Leaving Liverpool at what was assumed to be their peak – he had just helped them win their first European Cup in 1977 – to join a team sixth in the Bundesliga was demonstrative of both Keegan’s single-mindedness and capacity to challenge himself. He also quadrupled his salary, reflecting the economic state of English football at the time.

View image in fullscreen Keegan with the ball at his feet for Hamburg in the 1977-78 Bundesliga season. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

Hamburg was not an initial success. Jealous teammates held meetings to get him kicked out of the club and, according to Keegan, refused to pass to him. His nadir came at Christmas 1977 when, in a festive-season friendly, unhappy at his plight and frustrated with over-physical treatment from the Lübeck defender Erhard Press, Keegan punched him on the jaw and subsequently knocked him out, receiving an eight-week ban as punishment. Yet, a year later, he won his first Ballon d’Or and went on to lead Hamburg to their first Bundesliga title since 1960.

Keegan embraced Germany, learning the language and was nicknamed “Mighty Mouse”, a tribute to his astonishing strength given his diminutive size. His first daughter, Laura, was born there but his finale, a European Cup final that would have sealed Hamburg’s place in history, was a sad one, ending as it did in defeat to Nottingham Forest. Having won three league titles, two Uefa Cups, an FA Cup and European Cup at Liverpool, the Bundesliga title would be the last trophy Keegan ever won. He was just 29 years old.

Keegan made a typically unconventional choice in joining Southampton, a promising yet small-market team under a talented, persuasive manager in Lawrie McMenemy. Keegan propelled them to a top-six finish and qualification for Europe, but they faded to seventh in the second season and Keegan, disillusioned, made a decision that would define the second half of his professional life.

Newcastle were in one of their periodic financial and footballing crises and in the old Second Division when, with money from brewers Scottish & Newcastle, they persuaded him to join in 1982. His father’s links to the north-east and reverence for Newcastle players such as Jackie Milburn were an emotional pull on Keegan, but one that cost him his England career. The manager, Bobby Robson, didn’t feel it appropriate to pick a second-tier player for England and Keegan, still captain and by far the most iconic national team player, learned from the press he had been “dumped”. He felt “betrayed, hurt and humiliated”.

Crowds doubled at St James’ Park with Keegan’s arrival and Newcastle were promoted as champions in Keegan’s second season, 1983-84, by which point he had already decided to quit playing at the age of 33. Typically impulsive, it was when Mark Lawrenson outsprinted Keegan to dispossess him during an FA Cup tie at Liverpool that he decided he would finish his career at the end of the season.

View image in fullscreen Keegan in action for England in May 1979. His international playing career ended in acrimonious fashion. Photograph: Peter Robinson/Empics Sport/PA

Keegan and family, which now included his second daughter, Sarah, born in 1982, decamped to his Marbella villa and, other than periodic business deals and discussions about a long-held dream to launch a Soccer Circus, he embraced retirement. Yet endless rounds of golf failed to satisfy. The family had moved back to his Hampshire home when Sir John Hall, a dynamic north-east businessman, called in 1992, begging Keegan to help Newcastle avoid relegation to the third tier and potential liquidation. Despite having watched no football for years, Keegan accepted. He threatened to quit after a few games but stayed to keep Newcastle up and promptly announced that he wanted to build a dynasty to rival Liverpool and challenge for the Premier League title.

Most considered that quixotic and yet Newcastle won promotion to the Premier League as champions and with judicious youthful signings such as Andy Cole and Rob Lee, and veteran players such as Peter Beardsley, they came third and sixth in the top flight. So great was his authority, Keegan could even placate angry fans on the steps of St James’ Park when the club sold Cole to Manchester United.

With that money the club signed David Ginola and Les Ferdinand and won nine of their first 10 games in 1995-96, often in thrilling fashion, establishing a seemingly unassailable 12-point lead by January. But a crucial defeat at home to Ferguson’s United in March 1996 and the Scot’s repeated use of psychological barbs seemed to weigh heavy on Keegan as his team’s form disintegrated. A dramatic yet debilitating 4-3 defeat at Liverpool led Sepp Blatter to write to Keegan but the sight of him slumped over advertising hoardings as Liverpool scored a last-minute winner suggested the toll was too much.

Keegan eventually cracked, denouncing Ferguson in his famous TV interview. “You can tell him now, we’re still fighting for this title and I’ll tell you, honestly, I will love it if we beat them. Love it!” United won the title with four points to spare.

View image in fullscreen Keegan (left) during a Fulham training session at Roehampton in 1999. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Keegan initially seemed determined to rebuild as the club signed Alan Shearer for a world-record £15m and they beat United 5-0 at St James’ Park that autumn, but Keegan quit soon after, outraged that a city banker preparing the club for flotation had issued him an ultimatum to sign a contract. Football’s new era seemed untethered from the idealistic foundational values imbued in him by Shankly.

Keegan seemed done with football until the now-disgraced Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed used speculative talks about his much-vaunted Soccer Circus to persuade him to become chief operating officer and eventually manager of Fulham in the third tier. He almost seemed at his happiest as the club accelerated to promotion, but his time was interrupted by a national crisis when Glenn Hoddle was sacked as England manager for making offensive comments about disabled people. The clamour for Keegan to take over was indicative of his popularity with ordinary fans. However, it proved a decision he came to greatly regret, taking in a humiliating Euro 2000 group-stage exit and ending with him resigning in the toilets after an ignominious defeat against Germany in England’s last game at the old Wembley Stadium. It was, he conceded, a job beyond his abilities.

That said, Keegan was happy to take on Manchester City in the old First Division, getting them promoted to the Premier League as champions with 99 points. He remained at the club for four years, an almost unprecedented period of stability at the club at that time. When he finally left City he seemed to be done with coaching and finally launched his Soccer Circus in Glasgow, though it closed after a few years. Yet there was to be one last comeback at Newcastle under the ill-starred ownership of Mike Ashley, which proved a disaster and lasted just eight months.

The idea that a high-minded, old-fashioned football manager schooled by Shankly could coexist with a modern businessman as ruthless as Ashley and his cast of minions running the club always seemed improbable. When he walked away from the job, eventually winning a lengthy and bitter constructive dismissal claim, it was to be Keegan’s last act in football. So acrimonious was the departure that he was only able to return in disguise to attend a function at the club.

The current regime made clear Keegan was always welcome back at St James’ Park. That was after his stage four cancer had been revealed in a series of speaking engagements in May 2026, one of which in Newcastle was, in retrospect, a heartfelt farewell to the fans to whom he had always felt closest. After that draining but exhilarating evening Keegan’s associates reported that he was in high spirits, energised by the reconnection with the fans who loved him most.

It was to prove Keegan’s final goodbye. Football, as he observed, had given him everything except for a happy ending.

Sports.title: A big red speaker, Louis Vuitton trophy trunks and a tattoo bet – how Spain celebrated World Cup win
Sports.content:
On the night that Spain won their first World Cup in 2010, Rodrigo Hernández was on camp somewhere lost in the woods of Connecticut. He had been canoeing when the selección beat Germany in the semi-final, upset to have missed it, and for the final he convinced one of the supervisors to let him watch, alone, on a mini-laptop in the hut where the staff slept. When Andrés Iniesta scored the winning goal in the 116th minute, he ran off screaming, doing laps of the lake. He was 14.

On the night that Spain won their second World Cup 16 years later, Rodrigo Hernández was back in the US, not so far from there. When Ferran Torres scored the winning goal in the 106th minute, he ran off screaming in a straighter line and accompanied this time: towards the corner where his other family were. And then, when it ended, when the fighting finished too, he collected the trophy, pausing just long enough for Donald Trump to leave centre stage before lifting it, his timing perfect even here.

It wasn’t the only trophy he had, but those could be handed over and this could not. By the time Rodri departed at 9.38pm eastern time, the last man out of the dressing room at the New Jersey New York Stadium, he couldn’t carry them all: walking with him, just ahead, Ladis had to lend a hand. A football team is never just the players, nor even just the coaches. When he departed the dressing room nine minutes earlier, the same happened for Pau Cubarsí. Nuria helped him, their boy: just 19, looking like a kid down here in the stadium in real life but not on the pitch where he’s a leader. Luis de la Fuente was accompanied by Paloma.

Rodri came with the trophy for the tournament’s best player too. Cubarsí had the young player award, Unai Simón the Golden Glove. They also had two World Cups, every Spain player did: a replica of their own in a black Louis Vuitton trophy trunk, not easy to fit under an arm, and another in Lego. Rodri had three: both of those and the cup. They departed laden down, great big plastic bags full, pieces of the history they made. Shirts, in red and yellow and blue and white. Balls, boots. They had cut the net and taken pieces of that too. They had been given rings, NBA style.

View image in fullscreen Mikel Merino holds a replica of the trophy in the dressing room after Spain’s triumph. Photograph: Alex Pantling/Fifa/Getty Images

Before the final began, Marc Cucurella had sneaked off towards the touchline and buried a coin in the pitch, like that other left-back Joan Capdevila had done in 2010. Iniesta had been out there, his name chanted, as he showed the cup to the stands. After it, Sergio Ramos brought it back again. Dashing out, excitedly kissing it, he placed it on the plinth for this new generation, achieving the impossible in emulating them, to go and collect. One by one they passed, Borja Iglesias and Lamine Yamal among the most evasive in shaking Trump’s hand, until Rodri took the trophy and lifted it to the sky.

Nico Williams went to find his mum in the front row and handed over his medal. Lamine Yamal had made his way across to Lionel Messi, who was sitting but who stood for him, embracing the boy in the bath, the successor: a rite of passage, an image that will be for ever. The actor Javier Bardem was hugging Iglesias, his new friend and idol. Ferran Torres was talking about a “great liberation”: he had suffered, felt how cruel this game could be, how people could be too, but he said: “Destiny is written: God gives to those who deserve.” And Keyne was, well, Keyne. In the dressing room – the same one, Cucurella noted, where he had been at last year’s Club World Cup – the champagne was cracked open.

It was brief – the flight to Spain was scheduled for 11pm and they wanted to get back – and soon they were on their way again. Behind the screen, along the corridor they came, way down in the depths and the half-light of the stadium. The president, the staff, all the players; the many, many people who made this so. Iglesias carried a bag so big it was like he was a student taking his washing home, and he was struggling to stop that box slipping. In the other hand he wheeled a big red speaker. Now playing: Dirty Cash (Money Talks) by PAWSA & Adventures of Stevie V. Lamine Yamal came, via the anti-doping room, in orange sunglasses, four chains, black cap on backwards. He didn’t wear his medal, but most did, thick discs round their necks. And commemorative shirts, ordered up in case.

View image in fullscreen Spain’s Lamine Yamal and Argentina’s Lionel Messi embrace after the match. Photograph: Jeenah Moon/Reuters

Back in Dallas, at a celebration after the semi-final victory, someone had joked to the federation president, Rafael Louzán, that the shirts should say world champions on one side and Finalissima winners on the other, two trophies in one. Tempting, but these bore just the one trophy, “Spain 26” on the back. The war in the Middle East had prevented the Finalissima from going ahead in Doha as scheduled in March and every time another option was offered, Argentina said no, the impression that of a team, a federation, running scared. “Good job we didn’t play,” Emi Martínez had said then, after they scraped past Mauritania in a hastily arranged friendly that filled the hole. “If we had played [Spain] like this …”

Something like this might have happened. Not just because Argentina played like this but because Spain made them play like this. “We gave them a battering,” came the verdict from one of those heading out of the dressing room. This wasn’t just a win; this was more. Has a 1-0 ever been as dominant? There was a moment late in the game, still at 0-0, when the Spain fans chanted: “Look at them! Look at them! How they shit themselves!” and they weren’t wrong. Argentina could not get out all game; as Spain turned the screw, still less, the goal seemingly inevitable; the surprise was that it hadn’t come yet, that there would be just one. When it did it came as a liberation but also an act of irresistible logic.

View image in fullscreen Ferran Torres scores the only goal of the World Cup final. Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty Images

Torres’s shot was Spain’s 20th. Argentina didn’t manage one until the 115th minute. They didn’t manage any on target, all game. Across 900 World Cup games for which Opta has the stats, it is only the third time that a team has failed to shoot. And this in the final. They had done to Argentina what they did to France and to everyone, choking them. For the whole tournament Spain had an xG against of 0.3 per game. “If my gloves could talk, they would say they didn’t have much work to do,” Simón said. “Many teams depend too much on the back line,” Aymeric Laporte said, but not Spain.

This was the triumph of a collective, of a group; it ended in New York, but it was built in Chattanooga and beyond, over 51 days. It is the triumph of an idea, a conviction and of a coach too: a victory for De la Fuente and the system he leads and the system that made him. He began his coaching career at Deportivo Alavés in the third tier, where he lasted just 11 games. It was November 2011 when he left and he has not had a club job since. For months, no one returned his calls. He was on the dole for a year and a half until he saw an advert for a job: the Spanish federation was looking for a coach for the youth system. He started in the under-17s. He won the European Championship with the under-19s and the under-21s. Then he won it with the senior side; now he has won the World Cup.

“They asked me what there is left to win; we said the next game in September because they’re insatiable,” he insisted afterwards. Simón said: “The manager is outstanding; he has been our leader.” Cucurella, meanwhile, was in trouble. He had promised that if Spain won the World Cup, he would get a tattoo of De la Fuente’s face and now he had to decide where to put it to minimise the damage, the flight home an opportunity to think. Not least to think what a fool he had been.

View image in fullscreen Marc Cucurella is to have a tattoo of Luis de la Fuente’s face after Spain’s win. Photograph: Lisi Niesner/Reuters

“I said: ‘You made a bad mistake’,” the coach joked. “But it’s not like I am so horrendously ugly that you have to put it somewhere it can’t be seen. And they are men of their word.” For all the laughs, that final line really mattered, and he knows: 10 of them played with him at junior level. The first title he ever won was the Under-19 Euros in 2015. In the middle of his midfield that day was Rodrigo Hernández.

Eleven years on, 16 since he watched Spain’s first World Cup win, motivation sought and identification found in what they achieved, Rodri was back in the US. The embodiment of that idea, a player who approached perfection here, no one played more passes nor made more tackles than him. No one had his weight either, the captain leading Spain out and leading them back too. Like so many of his teammates at a tournament that was an expression of justice and vindication too, he had suffered for this, a torn cruciate ligament overcome.

“It doesn’t matter if you fall, there’s always a reason to get up again,” he said and now he had it right here in his hands. It was 9.40pm when he boarded the bus bound for the airport, carrying the actual World Cup.

Sports.title: Argentina players face bans as Fifa opens investigation into World Cup final brawls
Sports.content:
Fifa has opened an investigation into the violent scenes that followed Spain’s World Cup final win on Sunday, with several Argentina players facing bans.

Nahuel Molina appeared to strike Spain’s captain Rodri in the stomach as he ran on to the pitch following the final whistle, while there was also a large melee on the halfway line, where Leandro Paredes appeared to grab Eric García by the throat before throwing Gavi to the ground.

Parades was subsequently shown a red card by the referee, Slavko Vincic, who had also sent off Enzo Fernández towards the end of normal time, as well as booking three other Argentina players and the head coach, Lionel Scaloni.

“Following an assessment of the relevant match reports for the Fifa World Cup final between Spain and Argentina, and in line with article 36 of the Fifa Disciplinary Code (FDC), the Fifa Disciplinary Committee has appointed a Disciplinary and Ethics Prosecutor to investigate potential breaches of the FDC with regard to the post-match incidents,” Fifa said in a statement.

Fifa is also investigating Argentina’s conduct after their semi-final win over England, when their players celebrated with a banner proclaiming “Las Malvinas son Argentinas”, which was smuggled into the Atlanta Stadium by supporters.

Fifa prohibits players or teams making political statements, so those involved could be banned.

Sports.title: Nearly two million people join Spain’s World Cup celebrations in Madrid
Sports.content:
Almost two million Spaniards, many still bleary-eyed and feeling a little delicate after the country’s historic World Cup victory against Argentina, descended on central Madrid on Monday night to welcome the triumphant national team home.

La Roja, who beat Argentina 1-0 in the final in New Jersey on Sunday night, were afforded the first of many heroes’ welcomes when they touched down at Madrid’s Barajas airport at 2.30pm local time on Monday.

Spain’s captain, Rodri, waved the trophy aloft as he emerged from the plane, his medal from the previous night around his neck. The team posed for a photo before heading into terminal four where hundreds of delighted fans, many in Spain strips and carrying the country’s red-and-yellow rojigualda flag, waited and hoped for a glimpse of the freshly minted champions.

Their first stop was an audience with King Felipe, Queen Letizia and their daughters, Princess Leonor and Princess Sofía, at the Zarzuela palace, northwest of Madrid, where the king paid tribute to their talent and determination.

“It’s been an epic triumph,” he said. “It’s been a privilege and a joy for the four of us to see you play in the final and to be able to celebrate with you that moment of lifting the cup, with immense thanks from all of Spain.”

Felipe also praised their fortitude, saying: “You’ve suffered, you’ve come home bruised and tired, you’ve endured some criticism, but what is all that compared with the joy of bringing the cup home?”

View image in fullscreen Thousands of Spain supporters gather at Plaza de Cibeles in Madrid on Monday. Photograph: Richard Zubelzu/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

The team’s next meeting was a visit to the Moncloa palace – the office and residence of the prime minister – to see Pedro Sánchez. The socialist prime minister offered the players and technical staff “massive thanks … for the game, for the effort and for the victory”.

Speaking at the Moncloa palace, Rodri said that “winning for you country is the most beautiful thing there is”. He added: “This generation grew up watching [Iker] Casillas and [Andrés] Iniesta lift the cup [in 2010] and having been able to do that today is the biggest thing you can do in football.”

The highlight for the fans – who braved the 34C evening heat – was the victory parade that wound its way from Moncloa to the Plaza de Cibeles just outside Madrid city hall. They crowded into the square, some sheltering from the sun under umbrellas, as the team approached in an open-topped bus. The central government’s delegate in Madrid put attendance along the route at around 1.8 million.

Madrid’s mayor, José Luis Martínez Almeida, told Radio Nacional de España that the capital had been working to give the team the homecoming they deserved. He also hailed the peaceful and joyous scenes that had greeted Spain’s victory on Sunday night.

View image in fullscreen Rodri carries the World Cup at Barajas airport on Monday. Photograph: Sergio R Moreno/GTRES/Shutterstock

“Even though there were thousands and thousands of people on the streets last night, there were practically no incidents in the city,” he said.

“We’re getting everything ready for tonight … The thing we’re focusing on is how to celebrate and greet a team that will live for ever in our memory.”

The victory – Spain’s second men’s World Cup win after their triumph against the Netherlands in South Africa in 2010 – was seen by hundreds of thousand of Spaniards who followed the match in bars, parks, fairgrounds, bullrings, and on giant screens in the centre of Madrid. The Spanish press have hailed it as “a unique collective experience” made possible by a young team that reflects all that is best about a modern, diverse and determined country.

The win has also been enthusiastically hailed by the country’s political class.

“WE ARE WORLD CHAMPIONS!!” Sánchez wrote in a social media post. “What an amazing national squad. Thank you, team.”

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of Spain’s conservative People’s party, was equally free with the capital letters. “Well-deserved WORLD CHAMPIONS! Values, hard work, humility, and faith. You have made history. There are no limits for this team … Long live Spain!!!” he wrote on X.

Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, also offered his congratulations to the team for carrying “the flag of Spain so far and so high”.

The Spanish postal service, Correos, has announced the creation of a special stamp to commemorate what it called “one of the greatest achievements in the history of Spanish sport”. The red-coloured stamp will bear the word CAMPEONES and feature two stars – one for each of Spain’s World Cup victories.

Sports.title: The 2026 World Cup was full of spectacle, scandal and compromise | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
Perhaps it’s too early, with the shreds of gold tape still fluttering through the New Jersey sky, to make a proper assessment. That will only come when everything has sunk in properly, when memories have had the chance to settle and shape themselves, when the consequences of certain events have become clear. But let’s try anyway to make some sort of assessment of where the World Cup that ended with Leandro Paredes grappling with Gavi ranks historically.

The Balogun Affair could yet have major consequences. At the moment, it feels that the world has moved on, but that’s the nature of tournaments. They have a momentum of their own, a drive towards the finish that tends to sweep everything else aside. But there can be little doubt that the bending before political pressure, sweeping aside 64 years of precedent to ensure a particular player could take the stage, just as Gianni Infantino had done with Cristiano Ronaldo, just as he had done in gerrymandering the qualification criteria for the Club World Cup to ensure Lionel Messi played, represents a milestone.

Perhaps in the future we will simply accept the principle that famous players get dispensation because making money is more important than justice or the good of the game – the prioritisation of revenue generation has been a feature of the 2026 tournament – or perhaps this will stiffen the sinews of opposition to Infantino; it’s been notable, for instance, how many British politicians – and some American ones – have taken to criticising Fifa and its president. An immediate consequence could be the expansion of the World Cup to 64 teams as Infantino looks to shore up his base, particularly given the damage US (and Canadian) immigration policy has done to his claims to be a champion of the global south.

Other issues that have sunk into the mulch of games will surely resurface. The treatment of Iran, for instance, was scandalous, and sets a worrying precedent. Ticket prices may be lower at the 2030 World Cup, but the idea that a reasonable proportion should be available to the regular fans who go to league football every week is now gone. The World Cup is no longer a mass movement but a luxury event.

The price paid by the host cities, similarly, will only become truly apparent in retrospect. That is financial, but it’s also social. In the US and Canada, there have been street sweeps of the homeless, people with very little deprived of what few possessions they have, ID and medication. In Mexico, there has been an outcry about water extraction and environmental damage linked to World Cup projects.

The Italian newspaper la Gazzetta dello Sport ran a double page on Saturday calling the World Cup a “disaster”, outlining certain major issues: ticket prices, Balogun, the weather, the increase in games, the decrease of rest. That may be an overstatement, but what followed really was a disaster as the newspaper found its ticket allocation for the final slashed from five to two. It’s not entirely clear whether the two were linked, but the idea that a media outlet could be denied access for rejecting the official narrative that this World Cup has been the greatest ever is dystopian.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk: World Cup Edition Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

That fitted the generally contemptuous attitude of Fifa towards the media at this tournament. While some venues – notably Houston and Atlanta – went out of their way to be welcoming, basic organisation and facilities were the worst for at least six World Cups. Quite understandably, nobody in the real world cares about journalists and whether the wifi works, but it’s indicative of a more general approach: fans are revenue units to be milked mercilessly; the media an irritating imposition.

The football, meanwhile, was good but not great. There were a number of fine and dramatic games – Brazil v Japan, Morocco v the Netherlands, England v Mexico, Argentina v Cape Verde, Norway v Côte d’Ivoire, Belgium v Senegal, Norway v Brazil, Argentina v Egypt – but unfortunately almost all of them were in the last 32 or last 16. The quarter-finals were not especially inspiring. Argentina’s win over England in the semi was thrilling and involved a collapse that will be discussed for years, but Spain’s win over France was almost too easy; Spain quickly established a degree of superiority over the French that was never really challenged.

And the final was dismal, an awful affair. The right team won, in their familiar bloodless way, but the grim spectacle was a direct consequence of the indulgence shown Argentina earlier in the tournament. The ending, inevitably, colours what went before, and drags this tournament behind 2022 and 2018, let alone the glorious World Cups of the 1980s or 1998. Posterity can judge where exactly in the middle rank it sits, whether above or below 2014 and 2006. It was not great but it was good and, beyond the Fifa bluster, that’s fine.

Sports.title: Football Daily | A desperate grab for attention. This is the way the World Cup ends
Sports.content:
AND BREATHE …

Maybe Donald Trump was simply confused. He must have seen the ticker tape, a group of men cavorting around an American field clad in red and thought he’d stumbled into one of his Maga rallies. That is the only logical explanation for his bizarre behaviour on the champions’ plinth in (a stadium near) New York as Spain hoisted their freshly won trophy aloft, Trump having to be dragged off the stage by notorious wallflower Gianni Infantino as Rodri exhibited his trademark composure, patiently waiting to bask in his team’s glory moment. This is the way the Geopolitics World Cup ends, not with a bang but a desperate grab for attention from the US president.



The GWC final had already witnessed its own on-field disgrace of course, in the shape of Argentina’s shameful performance. La Albiceleste tarnished their proud footballing history with a display completely devoid of ambition, pride and, well, quality. No shots in regulation time, no shots on target in the entire 120 minutes and Enzo Fernández sent off in ignominy. Even Lionel Messi embarrassed himself for snitching to Slavko Vincic, pleading with the referee to brandish a red card after Marc Cucurella dared to put his hand to his mouth. The full-time scenes were even more debasing for Argentina, losing their heads in such a manner it made their first-half roughhouse tactics in the semi-final against England look like child’s play. This is the way the Geopolitics World Cup ends, not with a bang but a thump from Leandro Paredes. Stay classy, lads.



With no little hyperbole, Trump proudly proclaimed the GWC to have been “one of the greatest events of any kind ever held”. Does that sentiment hold muster? Well, it’s certainly been the biggest World Cup ever, with more teams, more matches, even more hosts than ever before. But of the 104 games (up from 64 in 2022), many have felt like a slog. UK readers, can you look Football Daily in the eye and truthfully say you stayed up until 3am to watch the conclusion of Ecuador 0-0 Curaçao? There has been plenty to enjoy, of course. Cape Verde were a genuine breath of fresh air, the only nation to play Spain and come away unscathed, while their near-miss in the last 32 against Argentina will be forever etched in World Cup folklore – oh what might have been but for Messi’s genius. We hope to see the Cape Verde lads back in 2030. Belgium’s late comeback to down Senegal was pure cinema, while England’s 6-4 win over France will live longer in the memory than a third-place playoff should simply for its pure weirdness.

Speaking of the Three Lions, who will ever forget Mexico and the Battle of the Azteca? Not Dan Burn and certainly not us. FD also enjoyed Mauricio Pochettino’s swashbuckling USA USA USA side in this tournament before Trump’s attempted assist for Folarin Balogun backfired spectacularly and the co-hosts became co-toast. Ultimately, perhaps a tired final in which the better team were stifled by one that refused to play the game entirely was fitting of the tournament as a whole. It was both exhaustive and exhausting and, as a footballing public we have discovered there is such a thing as too much football. The fatigue is real. Thank god it’s all over …. Now, who fancies watching South Shields versus Harrogate in pre-season on Tuesday? Anyone?

LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE

There’s no more live football for a little bit, so for now you’ll have to make do with the GWC farewell news blog.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“I like a lot of them artists, but I thought it was crap” – Wayne Rooney with a magnificently succinct live review of the GWC half-time show.

View image in fullscreen Even a frontline of Ronaldinho, Madonna and Ronaldo couldn’t get Rooney’s juices flowing. Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty Images

double quotation mark Football 1-0 Sh!thousery. Thank god anti-football failed” – Paul Landaw.

double quotation mark Can you start a Stop Argentina campaign? – Gordon MacLeod.

double quotation mark When will the photograph of Donald Trump giving a baby Gianni Infantino a bath surface?” – Krishna Moorthy.
