World.title: Attacks on Ukrainians in Poland rise, police data show
World.content:
The number of nationality-motivated attacks in Poland is steadily increasing, according to data provided to the Polish press by the National Police Headquarters.

 

This month has already seen widespread coverage of a vulgar attack on teenage girls from Ukraine on a municipal bus in Bielsko-Biała. An adult man verbally abused, threatened and insulted the girls for no other reason than that they were speaking Ukrainian.

And this is just one of 180 incidents that were reported to the police in the first half of 2026.

Alarming figures on attacks

Data shows that the scale of aggression against Ukrainians in Poland has risen sharply.

In 2024, Ukrainians living in Poland filed 267 reports of alleged hate crimes. In 2025, that number rose to 275. The 180 reports filed in the first half of 2026 already represent an increase of more than 30% compared with the same period last year, and nearly 35% compared with 2024.

Political blame game

Politicians are trading accusations over who is to blame for the rise in attacks.

Interior and Administration Minister Marcin Kierwiński wrote on X: "Kaczyński, Braun and Czarnek are doing a great deal to ensure that the brown wave spreads across Poland. The victims are both Poles and foreigners. I have a message for all those who have fallen in love with hatred: the police will always respond firmly. Zero tolerance!".

Opposition Law and Justice (PiS) spokesperson Rafał Bochenek said that "Every form of violence and aggression, both physical and verbal, especially against vulnerable people, including children, should be unequivocally condemned and the perpetrators held to account."

He argued that Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Interior and Administration Minister Marcin Kierwiński bear responsibility for such attacks: "Donald Tusk and Marcin Kierwiński have not only deliberately downplayed the rise in aggression on Polish streets so far, they are directly responsible for the brutalisation of public life in Poland".

Polish-Ukrainian relations deteriorate

Ukrainian activist Natalia Panchenko, from the organisation Stand With Ukraine in Poland, sought to ease tensions between Ukrainians and Poles in a Facebook post following the case in which teenage Ukrainian girls were subjected to abusive comments on a municipal bus in Bielsko-Biała.

"The state is fighting xenophobia. Poland stands for the rule of law. Law enforcement agencies, the courts and the law operate here. That is why we should seek to hold the individual perpetrator to account, rather than projecting his actions onto an entire nation. I know many Poles who have been helping Ukraine for years. (...) Some idiot on a bus is not the whole of Poland. Just as any criminal among Ukrainians is not the whole of Ukraine," she wrote.

World.title: Emergency farming law: reintroduction of two banned pesticides splits political parties
World.content:
French MPs are due to vote on Monday evening on the emergency agriculture bill, whose final version was approved last Thursday by a joint committee (CMP). A piece of legislation whose adoption is far from a foregone conclusion.

 

Of the 78 articles contained in the bill, one in particular is splitting France’s political forces: the reintroduction, by way of derogation, of acetamiprid and flupyradifurone – two pesticides banned in France but authorised in the European Union – for certain struggling sectors.

Last year, the bill put forward by Senator Laurent Duplomb, which already envisaged the return of acetamiprid, ran into strong public opposition, leading to a widely supported petition. The provision was ultimately struck down by the Constitutional Council.

A divisive bill, even within the government

In an effort to rally his troops ahead of the vote, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu convened a meeting at Matignon on Monday with the main representatives of the government coalition (Renaissance, MoDem, Horizons, LR), the centrist Liot group, as well as ministers Annie Genevard, Monique Barbut, Mathieu Lefèvre and Laurent Panifous.

The Minister for Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut, said on Saturday that the reintroduction of banned pesticides remained "the main sticking point".

"To make this bill fail out of ideology, calculation or fear would utterly dash farmers’ hopes", argued Agriculture Minister Annie Genevard.

Renaissance MP Prisca Thevenot says that "it is urgent that [the bill] be passed and implemented" but that "out of 78 articles there is one that raises questions" and puts the legislation "in mortal danger". She is categorical: "Acetamiprid must not appear in this bill."

Prisca Thévenot listens to Emmanuel Macron during a meeting of the Council of Ministers, on Friday 21 July 2023 at the Élysée Palace in Paris AP Photo/Christophe Ena, Pool

Prisca Thevenot had previously recalled that the government could "always table an amendment to delete acetamiprid" before Monday’s final vote.

The secretary-general of Renaissance, Gabriel Attal, had also urged "the government to table a deleting amendment" for the article concerning acetamiprid, according to a Les Républicains (LR) MP speaking to AFP.

Late on Monday afternoon, people close to Sébastien Lecornu nonetheless confirmed that Matignon was not proposing to scrap this derogation, preferring to let Parliament "decide" the matter.

The current version of the bill is backed by the Rassemblement national (RN) as well as many right-wing and centrist MPs.

By contrast, most Horizons MPs "seem to favour removing acetamiprid", according to a source close to the talks. As for MoDem, while one source indicated that "the acetamiprid totem continues to raise questions for some MPs", no common position has yet been made public.

Environmental concerns

A year after the revolt against the Duplomb law, this new bill is once again dividing French society, at a time when the climate context is sharpening anxieties over environmental protection.

For the environmental association Générations Futures, bringing back banned pesticides would mark "the Senate’s deadly U-turn".

Conversely, the president of the Confédération générale des planteurs de betteraves sucrières (CGB), Franck Sander, believes that the reauthorisation "in a targeted and regulated way" of flupyradifurone "is an essential condition for our competitiveness when all the indicators are flashing red".

Related Study links exposure to agricultural pesticides to cancer risk

The reform of water storage for agricultural irrigation, provided for in the emergency agriculture law, is another source of contention. Several protests against this measure are planned this week, including a demonstration on Monday evening at Les Invalides.

Annie Genevard nonetheless considers this reform a "common-sense" measure. "If we give up on this emergency agriculture law, we condemn the French to imported food. I will not accept that", she said on X.

The vote on this bill in the National Assembly, ahead of its passage to the Senate on Tuesday, comes as recent heatwaves have pushed environmental issues back to the forefront of French concerns.

Almost a third of them (32%) now consider environmental protection a priority issue, according to a poll carried out for La Tribune Dimanche, a 12-point increase.

World.title: People’s photos are helping scientists record marine life in real-time in the Canary Islands
World.content:
With more than 85,000 recorded and validated sightings in the waters of the so-called ‘Lucky Islands’ or Macaronesia, scientists from the RedPROMAR project have recorded more than 5,000 species of living organisms in this part of the North Atlantic.

 

Dennis Rabeling, a diving instructor at Euro-Divers Lanzarote, is one of its main contributors. He dives every day and uploads thousands of photos of marine flora and fauna to the website of this European project, which is co-funded by the Government of the Canary Islands. He has contributed to the discovery of three species previously unknown in the Canary Islands, one of which is named after him: Gibberula Dennisi. “With RedPROMAR, if you upload your photos, you become another pair of eyes on the water. In this way, scientists can identify new species that we did not previously know lived here. Today, during a thirty-minute dive, we saw around twenty or thirty species, perhaps even more," he explains.

Through this project, ocean culture is brought into the classroom, and the classroom is brought closer to the sea. This year, secondary school pupils from Juan Francisco Rodríguez García’s class at IES Yaiza have studied how human activities affect the marine environment, recorded a podcast on tropicalisation and its consequences, and undertaken a field trip to Órzola, in the north of Lanzarote, to learn ‘in situ’ which species live in the sea and how RedPROMAR works.

“We’ve taught them about a tool which allows any member of the public, including them, to take a photo of a particular species and geotag it using the same app, in order to provide better scientific data and contribute to scientific research” Juan Francisco Rodríguez García Environmental educator and teacher, IES Yaiza

An experience their pupils will never forget. Aroa says, “I didn’t even know most of the species. I hadn’t heard those names before at all. Take the manatee, for example. When an animal tries to bother it, it releases a kind of purple ink to scare it away. It’s really amazing."

The total budget for the project is just under two million euros, of which 85% has been funded by the European Cohesion Policy and the remaining 15% by the Canary Islands Government.

The pieces of the photo jigsaw speak

This project began in the Canary Islands and has since expanded its scope to Cape Verde, Madeira and the Azores. Each geotagged photo is checked by a team of experts. Marc Martín Sola, a marine biologist at Gesplan and a technician with RedPROMAR, says that “citizen science data is like a jigsaw puzzle, in which observers provide us with small pieces that, taken individually, may not make sense”, but when put together, they are valuable to the scientific community and to the authorities.

“By putting all these pieces together, we can see things that we wouldn’t be able to see individually; for example, introduced species or protected species, and we can better assess a species’ distribution or breeding season” Marc Martín Sola Marine biologist at Gesplan and technician with RedPROMAR

The platform also serves as an early-warning system for the arrival of alien species and the proliferation of species linked to human activity or climate change. “There are specific times when we receive a lot of reports, a lot of sightings of a particular species, and this usually coincides with ‘arribazones’ (washed ashore) – the mass arrival of organisms, whether alive or dead, on the coast,” explains Marc. “In 2024, we had more than a hundred sightings in just a few months. "Citizen science enables us to detect and record these sudden surges that might otherwise go unnoticed by the scientific community and thus keep a record of when and where they have occurred," he concludes.

World.title: Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended
World.content:
On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

Advertising

On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

A decade ago, factions within the Turkish military, composed of rebellious officers and followers of the Islamic cleric Fethullah Gulen, launched a dramatic attempt to topple President Erdogan.

"I remember, as a soldier, those who started the coup," recalls Murat Aslan, an army officer at the time. "I had no idea that there were members of this organisation (Gulen followers); they were very secretive."

Erdogan tightens his grip

Now a security analyst at SETA, a pro-government think tank, Aslan describes the failed coup as a turning point that reshaped the course of Turkish democracy.

"The message was very clear. Turkish society collectively rejected it," said Aslan. "Thousands took to the streets; that's more than challenging, because you see tanks rolling and people trying to stop them, trying to capture the soldiers with their rifles. It takes more than courage." More than 250 people died resisting the coup.

In the aftermath, Erdogan imposed emergency rule and expanded his presidential authority through a sharply contested national referendum. "This military intervention actually consolidated the Erdogan-led government," Aslan added.

Turkey's military, relations with US to survive failed coup, ruling party vice-president

Hundreds of soldiers and officers faced prosecution as the government declared an end to the army's long history of political interference. Since 1960, the military had orchestrated three coups, the most recent in 1980.

A decade of purges and closures

In the wake of the failed takeover, tens of thousands were purged from state institutions, many never returning even after being cleared.

More than a thousand NGOs were shut down during two years of emergency rule. Milena Buyum, senior Turkey campaigner for Amnesty International, acknowledges the grave threat to democracy posed by the attempted coup: "The state has a responsibility to ensure the safety and security of its citizens and to investigate criminal acts like the ones carried out that night," said Buyum.

Turkey's Erdogan warms to Russia after West coup response

However, Buyum warns that many of the measures introduced under the state of emergency have since been written into ordinary law, permanently curtailing fundamental freedoms: "The right to freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and association: the impact on civil society was felt very sharply and starkly in the immediate aftermath of the coup, but that impact continues," said Buyum.

Ankara's alliances

The failed coup also drove a wedge into Turkey's long-standing alliance with the United States. "Ankara saw the hand of the United States behind the failed coup attempt," claims Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, who leads the Ankara office of the German Marshall Fund.

Even before the attempted coup, Erdogan's relations with President Barack Obama had been tense. Obama's belated support, offered only after the coup had failed, fuelled Ankara's suspicions of US complicity, particularly as Washington refused to extradite Fethullah Gulen, whom Erdogan blamed for orchestrating the plot. Gulen denied the accusation until his death in 2024.

Turks in France divided on failed coup

Unluhisarcikli observes that US-Turkish relations remained strained for years, while Erdogan gravitated towards Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose rapid show of support stood in sharp contrast to Washington's hesitation.

"Putin was among the first leaders, I believe even the first, to extend political support to the elected government in Ankara, and in those days I believe that support mattered greatly to President Erdogan," Unluhisarcikli said.

Rumours still persist in Turkey today that Moscow warned Erdogan on the day of the failed coup. Unluhisarcikli says it was only with the election of President Donald Trump, who shared Erdogan's animosity towards Obama and Joe Biden, that US-Turkish relations began to thaw, a shift highlighted at this month's NATO summit in Ankara. Yet the wave of mass arrests during the summit, enabled by post-coup emergency powers, served as a stark reminder that the shadow of the failed takeover still looms over Turkey.

World.title: US imposes new 50% tariff on many Canadian goods
World.content:
The tariffs will cover products including wine and hockey sticks, but not energy or fish. The move is the latest trade escalation between the US and its northern neighbor under the Trump administration.

US President Donald Trump's administration on Monday announced it was imposing 50% tariffs on a wide range of Canadian goods.

The White House said the tariffs would take effect in 30 days and cover "products ranging from wine to hockey sticks to cement."

Trump signed the three proclamations under Section 338 of the Tariff Act ​of 1930 — a nearly century-old trade law that allows for tariffs of up to 50% on imports from ​specific countries.

However, the new tariffs will not apply to energy, potash (used in agricultural fertilizer), fish, critical minerals and goods already covered by existing tariffs under Section 232 of the law which relates to national security.

White House accuses Canada of 'discriminatory treatment'

The White House said the move was a response to Canada's "discriminatory treatment" of American goods.

Specifically, it said Canada imposed tariffs and quotas on US-manufactured cars that it did not apply to cars from other countries, and it said all but two Canadian states and territories have restricted the distribution of American alcohol.

"Over the past year and a half, only two countries have chosen to retaliate against President Trump’s tariffs rather than negotiate a deal with the United States: the People’s Republic of China and Canada," the White House said.

How did Canada respond to the new US tariff plan?

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said the US tariffs are "in direct violation" of the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA), "the free trade agreement between Canada, the United States and Mexico."

Carney said Canada has made proposals to "modernize" CUSMA and "we stand ready to intensify those discussions in the coming weeks."

Ontario Premier Doug Ford condemned the proposed US tariffs, warning that they would have economic consequences on both sides of the border.

In a post on X, Ford vowed to continue advocating for Ontario's interests, arguing that Canada should match any US tariffs with equivalent countermeasures.

He said, “I’ll never stop fighting to protect Ontario. If these tariffs proceed, Canada should respond tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar.”

Candace Laing, president and CEO of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, described the Trump administration's latest tariff measures as "regrettable" in comments to AP news agency.

She urged both countries to use the 30-day period before they take effect "to make meaningful progress in advancing formal talks."

The implications of the tariffs extend beyond Canada, according to Scott Lincicome, vice president of general economics at the libertarian Cato Institute in Washington, D.C. He warned in comments also to AP that the measures would inject "massive uncertainty" into the global economy and affect a range of US trading partners.

"We crossed the Rubicon," Lincicome said, describing the use of Section 338 as "the nuclear option for Trump tariffs."

Trump threatens new Canada tariffs as wildfire smoke spreads To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Wildfires add to growing US–Canada tensions

Trump has also suggested additional tariffs in response to Canadian wildfire smoke that has affected air quality in parts of the United States.

Although Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Carney attended the FIFA Club World Cup final together, US officials said their meeting was not intended to address trade issues.

The latest tariff measures reflect broader tensions between the two countries. Trump earlier in his second term mocked Canada and said it should be the 51st US state, sparking backlash from Canadians and pushback from Carney.

World.title: Iran war: US launches fresh strikes as Trump vows revenge
World.content:
07/21/2026 July 21, 2026 US military completes latest round of strikes on Iran

The US military said it completed another round of strikes against Iran, targeting military command centers, maritime capabilities, missile and drone launch sites, and air defense systems.

In a statement, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said the operation was aimed at degrading Iran's ability to continue attacks on commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important maritime trade routes.

CENTCOM said commercial shipping through the waterway remained ongoing despite the conflict. According to the US military, its forces have helped facilitate the transit of approximately 900 commercial vessels and 450 million barrels of crude oil through the strait since early May.

The US military also said its forces remain positioned to respond to what it described as Iranian aggression against civilian shipping, pledging to hold Tehran accountable for attacks on vessels navigating the strategic waterway.

World.title: Mexican drug lord ‘El Mayo’ sentenced to life without parole in US prison
World.content:
Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada, a co-founder of the Sinaloa cartel and one of the world's most notorious drug traffickers, was sentenced to life in a US prison.

Mexican drug trafficker Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole on Tuesday for co-founding and leading the notorious Sinaloa cartel.

Zambada was one of the most prominent Mexican drug traffickers to face sentencing in a United States court since Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman was sentenced to life in prison in 2019.

"The almost unimaginable amount of drugs attributable to him and the number of murders that we can document is enough to justify Congress's decision to make this a mandatory life sentence," US District Judge Brian Cogan said.

The 76-year-old Zambada apologized "for the harm I caused and for the example I set," urging future generations to "choose a different path."

Zambada apologizes before sentencing

He was arrested in July 2024 after he said he was kidnapped in Mexico and flown to Texas.

Zambada helped found and lead the Sinaloa cartel, becoming one of the most wanted figures for US intelligence and law enforcement agencies for decades.

According to prosecutors, he ordered torture and plotted murders, including the killing of his own nephew, as the cartel flooded the US with tons of cocaine, fentanyl, methamphetamine and other drugs.

U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said Zambada had spent nearly four decades 'poisoning American communities' for profit and ordering the murders of anyone who stood in his way, and that all ended with his sentencing Image: Leonardo Munoz/AFP

He pleaded guilty to charges that included engaging in a continuing criminal enterprise and racketeering conspiracy, acknowledging culpability for 85 underlying crimes. In exchange, prosecutors did not seek the death penalty.

"I grew up in an environment where violence and crime seemed normal, but now I know that's no excuse," Zambada said in court on Monday. "There comes a time when every person must take responsibility for their decisions. I didn't, and many people paid the price."

"El Chapo" partner joins cartel leaders serving life terms

Zambada's former partner "El Chapo" is already serving a life sentence in the United States.

He was convicted in 2019 and is serving a life sentence at the federal Supermax prison in Florence, Colorado.

Together they built the Sinaloa cartel into one of the world's most powerful drug trafficking organizations.

Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman was sentenced to ​life in prisonin 2019 Image: Paul Ratje/REUTERS

The Sinaloa cartel is one of six Mexican drug gangs that US President Donald Trump has designated as Foreign Terrorist Organizations.

Zambada was arrested with El Chapo's son, Joaquin Guzman Lopez, one of El Chapo's sons, who has pleaded guilty to federal drug charges. He has yet to be sentenced.

Zambada's arrest led to a splintering of the Sinaloa cartel, pitting his loyalists against backers of Guzman's sons, dubbed the Chapitos, or "little Chapos."

World.title: AliExpress hit with record EU fine
World.content:
The Chinese retailer has become the latest major online marketplace to face penalties under the EU’s Digital Services Act.

AliExpress said it plans to appeal a penalty imposed by European Union (EU) regulators, who found shortcomings in the firm's efforts to curb illegal, unsafe and counterfeit goods.

The largest Chinese e-commerce platform in the EU, AliExpress, has been fined €550 million ($629 million) for failing to tackle sales of illegal, unsafe and counterfeit products.

"The spread of counterfeit clothing, unsafe toys, dangerous cosmetics and other illegal and harmful products is not an unavoidable cost of shopping online - it is a failure by AliExpress to comply with its obligations under the Digital Services Act," European Commission Vice President Henna Virkkunen said on Monday.

It is the largest fine ever imposed under the Digital Services Act (DSA), which sets out clear rules for online services in the EU, targeting especially very large online platforms.

AliExpress said it will appeal the "disproportionate" fine, saying it considers the penalty excessive.

AliExpress faces October 20 deadline

The online retail giant, which belongs to the Alibaba Group, must pay the fine and has until October 20, to submit a plan to address the breaches. EU regulators will then review the plan, after which the company could face further penalties.

A year ago, AliExpress agreed to tighten controls on illegal and potentially dangerous goods, such as medicines and supplements. But the European Commission said the measures did not fully resolve its broader concerns.

The commission said AliExpress:

Failed in some cases to penalize traders selling illegal products, allowing them to continue operating on the platform.

Lacked sufficient staff to effectively review potentially illegal listings.

Inspectors faced excessive workloads, hampering oversight efforts.

Some illegal products were recommended or promoted before being removed from the platform.

But AliExpress said the EU's decision "ignores our sound risk management framework and the significant, proactive enhancements we have made."

The company also said it has worked with the Commission to meet its "evolving expectations."

DSA used to rein in Big Tech

According to the EU, AliExpress has 193 million users in the bloc, ahead of online fashion giant Shein and retailer Temu, which have 156 million and 130 million users, respectively.

"One in five Europeans say they shop once a month from Shein, Temu and AliExpress," Virkkunen said.

Temu was fined €200 million in May, while Elon Musk's social media platform X was fined in December last year, both for DSA violations.

World.title: England and Liverpool foortball legend Kevin Keegan dies aged 75
World.content:
English former striker and manager Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75 after a battle with cancer. He was a two-time European footballer of the year with Hamburg.

The death of Kevin Keegan, regarded as one of the greatest football players of his generation, was announced in a statement released by his family on Monday.

"It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75," the statement read.

"Kevin had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments. A double Ballon d'Or winner, Kevin was a much-loved husband, father and grandfather."

Born in Doncaster, South Yorkshire on February 14, 1951, Keegan got his big break when he was signed by Liverpool's legendary manager Bill Shankly in 1971.

At Anfield, Keegan struck up a striking partnership with Welshman John Toshack, going on to win the First Division title three times as well as the FA Cup, the UEFA Cup twice and the 1977 European Cup. He made 323 appearances, scoring 100 goals for Liverpool.

Success in the Bundesliga

From Merseyside, Keegan moved on to the Bundesliga's Hamburg, where he was twice named European Footballer of the Year, which is now called the Ballon d'Or, in 1978 and 1979. With Hamburg, he won the Bundesliga in 1978-79 and played in another European Cup final, a 1980 loss to Nottingham Forest. He left the club having scored 32 goals in 90 appearances.

Hamburg were among the former teams to pay tribute to Keegan in a statement on their website on Monday.

"In Kevin Keegan, world football loses one of its most defining figures. Hamburger SV will always cherish the memory of its former title-winning player and two-time Ballon d'Or winner," the statement said.

Our thoughts are with his family, his friends, and all those who shared his journey. Rest in peace, "Mighty Mouse."

Return to England

Following his stint in West Germany, Keegan returned to England with Southampton in the summer of 1980 before moving to Second Division Newcastle, helping the club win promotion back to the top flight – before retiring as a player.

He won 63 England caps, scoring 21 goals, playing at the 1982 World Cup and was also later captain of the national team.

Stepping into management

In 1992, Keegan moved into management at Newcastle, leading them into the Premier League and to within touching distance of the 1995-96 title, but they missed out to Manchester United.

The club also paid tribute to Keegan in a statement issued on Monday afternoon, describing him as "the beating heart of Newcastle for generations of supporters."

After leaving St James' Park in January 1997, a brief stint at Fulham followed before he became England manager in 1999. After overseeing a disappointing Euro 2000 campaign, Keegan resigned minutes after a 1-0 defeat by Germany in World Cup qualifying, the last match played at the original Wembley Stadium.

He later managed Manchester City, before returning to Newcastle.

Keegan's family had revealed in January that he had been diagnosed with cancer, which later spread to stage four.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

World.title: Russia says bus strike kills 5 in border region with Ukraine
World.content:
The strike comes as Ukraine launched more than hundreds of drones at Moscow after a Russian missile barrage on Kyiv, as President Zelenskyy sought to calm growing tensions over Ukraine’s military leadership.

Russia said Monday that a Ukrainian strike on a bus in the border region of Belgorod killed five civilians, including a minor, and left three others critically injured.

The attack came after a Ukrainian retaliatory strike on Moscow, with city officials reporting that more than 400 drones targeted the Russian capital.

The latest escalation followed Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities over the weekend.

Russian strikes targeted the eastern cities of Pavlograd and Kramatorsk in Ukraine Image: REUTERS

In eastern Ukraine, Russian attacks on Pavlograd and Kramatorsk killed two people in each city, according to local authorities.

Officials also reported one person killed in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia during Russian bombardment.

Both sides have previously denied targeting civilians.

Ukraine launches large-scale drone attack on Moscow

Ukraine targeted the Russian capital with more than 400 drones from Sunday into Monday, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said.

He added that most of the drones were intercepted, but Moscow region Gov. Andrei Vorobyov said at least 10 people were wounded by Ukrainian drones.

Several residential buildings and civilian infrastructure facilities were also damaged.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces were targeting Russian logistics facilities and an oil depot in the region.

"We are responding, justly, to every Russian strike against our cities and communities," Zelenskyy said in a post on X.

Ukraine rejects rumors of military leadership shake-up

Meanwhile, Ukraine's military publicly denied rumors that Zelenskyy was firing the chief of Ukraine's armed forces, Oleksandr Syrskyi.

Zelenskyy has faced criticism over the dismissal of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov last week.

There have been days of protests in Ukraine following Fedorov's removal, as a long-running dispute between the reform-minded minister and Syrskyi spilled into the open.

Zelenskyy appointed Yevhenii Khmara, the acting head of Ukraine's Security Service (SBU), as acting defense minister and asked parliament to approve him for the position.

On Monday, he posted several messages on social media showing him meeting with Ukraine's top military commanders to discuss the latest developments in the war, which has dragged on for more than four years.

World.title: Guterres to visit Cyprus as UN seeks to revive peace talks
World.content:
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres will visit Cyprus next week in what is seen as an effort to kickstart the stalled peace process. Why now? What is known about the plan? And what might be different this time round?

Monday marks the 52nd anniversary of Turkey's 1974 invasion of Cyprus, which led to the division of the island.

Five decades later, the Cyprus issue remains one of the world's longest-running unresolved disputes.

The United Nations announced last week that Antonio Guterres was due to visit Cyprus from July 27 to 29 — the first visit by a UN secretary-general in 16 years — in an effort to breathe new life into the stalled peace process.

A new UN push for progress

His visit marks the culmination of a renewed UN initiative that was launched after an informal enlarged meeting on Cyprus held in Geneva in March.

Since then, the UN secretary-general's personal envoy, Maria Angela Holguin, has held a series of consultations in Cyprus, Greece, Turkey, the United Kingdom and Brussels to assess whether the political conditions exist for meaningful negotiations to resume.

Antonio Guterres will visit Cyprus next week. It is the first visit to the island by a UN secretary-general in 16 years Image: Jean Marc Ferré/MAXPPP/IMAGO

During his stay in Cyprus, Guterres will hold separate meetings with President of the Republic of Cyprus Nikos Christodoulides and Turkish Cypriot leader Tufan Erhurman.

On July 29, the two leaders are expected to meet jointly with the UN chief at the residence of the UN Special Representative in the UN-controlled buffer zone.

UN initiatives in the past 25 years

The last time a UN secretary-general visited Cyprus was in 2010, when Ban Ki-moon sought to inject political momentum into negotiations between then President of the Republic of Cyprus Demetris Christofias and Turkish Cypriot leader Mehmet Ali Talat.

Both leaders came from left-wing political parties that supported a bizonal, bicommunal federation and were widely seen as having the political will to pursue a comprehensive settlement.

That momentum, however, faded only months later after Talat lost the Turkish Cypriot leadership election to Dervis Eroglu, while major disagreements over the core chapters of the negotiations remained unresolved.

Ban's efforts were preceded by the intensive engagement of Kofi Annan between 2002 and 2004, when the UN undertook its most ambitious effort to broker a comprehensive settlement of the Cyprus issue.

Former UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon (center) sought to inject some momentum into negotiations between the two sides in 2010. He is pictured here with President of the Republic of Cyprus Demetris Christofias (left) and Turkish Cypriot leader Dervis Eroglu Image: Katia Christodoulou/dpa/picture alliance

Annan became personally involved in the negotiations, presenting a series of revised versions of what became known as the Annan Plan.

The initiative culminated in simultaneous referendums in April 2004. The proposal was approved by a majority of Turkish Cypriot voters but rejected by 75.8% of Greek Cypriot voters.

Reports in the British media

The announcement of Guterres' visit comes amid reports that the UN is exploring a possible new framework for resolving the Cyprus issue.

The discussion gained momentum after Britain's The Independent reported on July 12 that Holguin was working on a revised settlement proposal.

According to the newspaper, the framework would retain the agreed model of a bizonal, bicommunal federation, as set out in relevant UN Security Council resolutions, while granting significantly greater autonomy to the two constituent states and limiting the powers of the federal government.

The report also claims that, in exchange for this broader autonomy, the Turkish Cypriot side would be expected to accept territorial adjustments, including the return of the fenced-off city of Varosha and the town of Morphou.

British newspaper 'The Independent' reported on July 12 that the UN secretary-general's personal envoy, Maria Angela Holguin (pictured here), is working on a revised settlement proposal for Cyprus Image: Kostas Pikoulas/IMAGO

It also suggests that new security arrangements are being considered that would allow Greek and Turkish troops to remain on the island under NATO command.

According to The Independent, the proposal seeks to bridge the gap between the Greek Cypriot commitment to a federal settlement and Turkey's long-standing support for a two-state solution.

The UN has neither confirmed nor denied the report.

Asked about it, President Christodoulides said that "not everything reported by the newspaper is accurate," adding that he expects further developments in the coming period.

What next?

Despite the expectations surrounding Guterres' visit, diplomats say the UN chief's immediate objective is not to discuss a draft settlement plan.

Diplomatic sources who spoke to DW believe the most likely outcome of the meetings next week will be the announcement of a new informal expanded meeting bringing together the leaders of Cyprus' two communities, representatives of Greece, Turkey and the UK — the island's three guarantor powers under the 1960 treaties — and the UN.

According to the same sources, such a meeting could take place in late August or early September. Unlike previous informal gatherings, however, the UN is said to be seeking a more structured process this time, with a clearer sequence of steps and a defined timeframe.

Why now?

Although Guterres' renewed engagement is inevitably linked to the final months of his second term, which ends in December, diplomatic sources believe the latest initiative is driven by more than his limited remaining time in office.

For the first time in years, they believe conditions for a renewed political dialogue may be emerging.

A key factor has been the election of Tufan Erhurman as Turkish Cypriot leader last October. Unlike his predecessor, Ersin Tatar, who advocated a two-state solution, Erhurman has said he is prepared to resume negotiations on the basis of a bizonal, bicommunal federation.

That change does not represent a shift in Turkey's official policy, nor does it resolve longstanding disagreements over security, guarantees, political equality or the continued presence of Turkish troops on the island.

It has, however, created conditions that allow the UN to test whether a meaningful return to negotiations is now possible.

What is the role of the EU?

Cyprus government spokesperson Konstantinos Letymbiotis believes Guterres' visit should also be viewed in the context of a broader increase in international diplomatic activity on Cyprus.

Antonio Costa (left) and Ursula von der Leyen (right) of the EU recently met Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan (center) in Ankara Image: Turkish Presidency/Murat Cetinmuhurdar/Handout/Anadolu/picture alliance

"The secretary-general's initiative, the European Union's stronger engagement and the appointment of Executive Vice-President Raffaele Fitto as the EU's envoy on Cyprus are creating new momentum," he told DW.

On July 8, European Council President Antonio Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen discussed the UN initiative with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, urging Ankara to make use of the renewed diplomatic momentum on Cyprus.

A few days later, the Commission appointed Raffaele Fitto as its special representative for the Cyprus issue.

The move was widely interpreted as a sign that Brussels intends to play a more substantive role in the process, while underlining that any future settlement must be fully compatible with EU law.

The EU's increased involvement is also closely linked to the broader trajectory of EU-Turkey relations.

From Brussels' perspective, progress on the Cyprus issue could facilitate movement on several key areas of cooperation with Ankara.

Conversely, the absence of progress continues to be one of the main obstacles preventing any meaningful upgrade in relations between the EU and Turkey.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

World.title: Why a 90-year-old treaty limits NATO in the Black Sea
World.content:
A 90-year-old treaty still shapes the balance of power in the Black Sea. As Ukraine fights on against Russia, can NATO project power into waters it can't enter freely?

Now more than four years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Black Sea has become one of Europe's key security frontiers. And yet, it is currently "quite empty of warships," Thomas de Waal, a senior fellow at Carnegie Europe, told DW. This, he said, "is a bit of a paradox." To understand that paradox, we first need to need to take a closer look at the map.

The Black Sea is bordered by six countries: Turkey, Bulgaria, Romania, Ukraine, Russia, and Georgia. The first three on that list are part of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, or NATO — the other three are not. To make matters more complicated, two of the latter three are at war with each other.

Narrow bottleneck to maneuver

Access to the Black Sea runs through a single, narrow bottleneck. To get there, a ship coming from the Mediterranean Sea would have to pass the Dardanelles Straits and the Bosporus, which crosses through the heart of Turkey's largest metropolis Istanbul.

At its narrowest point, the Bosporus is just 700 meters (0.4 miles) wide. For comparison, another critical passageway currently in the headlines is the Strait of Hormuz, which is approximately 33 kilometers (21 miles) wide at its narrowest point.

It is this geographic bottleneck to the Black Sea that makes it "an economic choke point," said de Waal. "Whoever controls the Turkish Straits also controls, to some extent, trade through the Black Sea and also has an enormous military advantage."

The Bosporus divides Istanbul into two sides, forming the boundary between Europe and Asia Image: Erdal3416/Depositphotos/IMAGO

Russia also has a special interest in the Black Sea, according to Daria Isachenko, a visiting fellow at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs. "A strong military position in the Black Sea for Russia is not an end in itself, but also a means to advance its geopolitical ambitions beyond and also strengthen its great power status."

The second part of the equation goes back to a treaty signed exactly 90 years ago.

Treaty that made Turkey gatekeeper

On July 20, 1936, representatives from just under a dozen countries gathered in the Swiss town of Montreux to settle a long-standing dilemma: How — and by whom — should these vital waterways be governed? They established the Montreux Convention, an agreement that essentially restored Turkey's sovereignty over the Dardanelles Strait and Bosporus. This came after years of international oversight, following the Ottoman Empire's defeat in the First World War.

Turkey reoccupied the Dardanelles Strait in July 1936, following the signing of the Montreux Convention Image: Topfoto/United Archives International/IMAGO

Negotiations resulted in a document of nearly 30 pages, which set the legal framework that governs the Turkish Straits to this day. The treaty keeps the straits open to passenger and commercial traffic during peacetime — crucial for the important trade route.

When it comes to military ships, Black Sea states are allowed to move their warships through the straits relatively freely. Any navy from outside the region faces restrictions on their fleet size, tonnage, and how long they are allowed to stay in the sea — no longer than 21 days during peacetime.

Special rules for war

During times of war, these rules become stricter. When Turkey is not part of the conflict, warships belonging to any nation involved in the fight are not allowed to pass through — a clause that has had profound consequences for the region since February 2022.

Russian warships passed through the Bosporus during the Syrian civil war Image: Ozan Kose/AFP

This special system of access rights keeps the Turkish government in a very powerful position. "The most privileged Black Sea state is Türkiye itself," Isachenko said.

It also helps explain why NATO doesn't maintain a continuous presence in the Black Sea — unlike in other waters such as the Mediterranean or the North Sea. "For NATO, Montreux is a constraint," Isachenko pointed out. "For Türkiye, it is an instrument to keep the balance in the Black Sea."

War in Ukraine tests Montreux Convention

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in late February 2022, the Montreux Convention arguably faced its greatest test in decades. A few days after the military operation began, Turkey invoked Article 19 of the treaty, which applies during wartime and restricts military ships belonging to countries engaged in the fight from passing through the straits.

Essentially, from that point onwards, neither Russia, nor Ukraine, could freely reinforce their naval forces in the Black Sea — with one exception: warships registered to a home port in the Black Sea could return to their base.

A Russian submarine passed through the Bosporus on February 13, 2022 — days before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine Image: Arife Karakum/AA/picture alliance

"I think the Montreux Convention and Turkey's policy at the beginning of the war was absolutely crucial in allowing Ukraine to survive," Thomas de Waal told DW.

He argued that it prevented Russia from adding more vessels to their Black Sea fleet, saying that "up to 30 Russian ships stayed outside." This, he added, contributed to Ukraine holding "the upper hand in the Black Sea."

Those restrictions may also have highlighted how warfare itself has changed, with Ukraine turning to drones and other modern technology not covered by the 1936 document. "Ukraine didn't build military vessels," according to Iulian Chifu, a Romanian foreign policy analyst. "It just shifted the generation of attack," he said.

The maritime treaty has also restricted the options available to Ukraine's supporters in the West. In 2024, the United Kingdom donated two minesweepers to Ukraine, which were unable to enter the Black Sea, according to the UK Ministry of Defence. That's because Turkey considers them to be "vessels of war," according to de Waal. Instead, the ships have been docked in Portsmouth, in southern England.

For de Waal, this illustrates Turkey's wider approach: "It's a very carefully constructed strategy," he said," in which Turkey basically says to other NATO countries: 'Leave us alone in the Black Sea, we will handle this.'"

Key to the convention's enduring relevance may be its long-standing recognition by states. "Turkey has come up with an arrangement, a regime, which Russia is not especially happy about, but accepts, and that's very important," he noted.

At a time when the international rules-based order has increasingly come under pressure, the Montreux Convention stands out as a rare example of a multilateral diplomatic mechanism that is still observed and respected 90 years after it was signed.

How is NATO adapting?

The geography of the Turkish Straits — plus their complex governance structure — have led to NATO rethinking how it can operate in the region. At times, the issue even creates some tension between its alliance members: "In the Black Sea," de Waal explained, "Turkey is very much Turkey first and NATO second."

This security logic, he argued, has shaped Turkey's message to its Western allies: "We don't want to see your permanent presence in the Black Sea, but Romania and Bulgaria have this shared Black Sea ownership, so you can support them."

Romania and Bulgaria joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007 Image: Denislav Stoychev/NurPhoto/picture alliance

As a result, greater focus has been placed on these two Eastern European states, which have been NATO members since 2004. However, some experts remain doubtful: "The military capabilities of Bulgaria and Romania," said Chifu, "are barely limited to their capacity of defending their territories."

Nevertheless, he argued that Romania had been "trying to improve our capabilities building ships," as well as purchasing military assets, with the aim of "enforcing our footprint in the Black Sea."

One example is the planned expansion of Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near the Romanian port city Constanța. Romania's government is expected to spend € 2.5 billion ($ 2.8 billion) on transforming it into the largest NATO military base in Europe — bigger than Ramstein, a US military base in Germany.

Earlier this month, the region was in the spotlight once again, as leaders of NATO's member states met in the Turkish capital Ankara for their annual summit. There, Turkey, Romania, and Bulgaria announced a trilateral task group for mine-clearing efforts to protect underwater infrastructure.



The 2026 NATO summit in Ankara was the second hosted by Turkey, after the 2004 summit in Istanbul Image: Turkish Presidency/Murat Cetinmuhurdar/Handout/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

What is next for the 90-year-old treaty?

The Montreux Convention is "quite an archaic document," de Waal told DW, pointing out that it still refers to the League of Nations — the UN's predecessor, which ceased to exist 80 years ago. "But I think no one wants to touch it," out of concern that it "opens a kind of Pandora's box when all the issues have to be renegotiated with Russia," he added.

"For Türkiye," said Isachenko, Montreux "also belongs to a number of founding treaties of the Turkish Republic." Beyond its role as a maritime access treaty, it reflects Turkey's core interests: "sovereignty, security and status," she added, so challenging Montreux means "dealing, revising and challenging" those core interests.

Security analyst Chifu stressed that he was "not revisionist" and believed the convention should stay in place while the Ukraine war rages on. "But after the war," he said, "we should reconsider very clearly how this is applied to our allies in NATO."

To him, the question of how exactly the treaty's clauses are applied and interpreted by Turkey remains a sore point.

"You have no option but to work with Turkey," is the key message de Waal took away from the recent NATO summit in Ankara. "You can't work without it," he said, referring to what he calls the strongest power in the Black Sea.

For the past nine decades, the Montreux Convention has outlasted wars, leaders, and entire generations. And as long as it lasts, Turkey holds sway over the Black Sea gateway.

Editors: Peter Hille and Don MacCoitir

World.title: Madrid ruge con la segunda estrella de España
World.content:
Casi dos millones de personas tiñen de rojo las calles de la capital para abrazar a los campeones del mundo en un día para la historia

Toda la fuerza con la que empujó todo un país a miles de kilómetros de donde la historia acontecía fue recibida ayer por los futbolistas y el cuerpo técnico de la selección española. La victoria de España en Nueva Jersey, que alcanzó, sumando todos los canales, 15.706.000 espectadores de media, provocó que las calles de Madrid, colmadas por casi dos millones de personas según Delegación de Gobierno, se convirtieran en un río de color rojo para abrazar a los nuevos campeones del mundo. Abuelos, hijos y nietos —algunos de estos últimos no vivían o no tienen el recuerdo de cuando España bordó su primera estrella en el pecho— vivieron eufóricos y con emoción desbordante cómo 26 muchachos unieron a todo un país.

Desde primera hora de la tarde la plaza de Cibeles comenzó a teñirse de grana. Paraguas en una mano, bocina en la otra y suministros de agua mínimos para soportar el calor sofocante, grupos y grupos de jóvenes se agolpaban en las vallas frente al escenario. Tampoco faltaron los cánticos. Un “campeones del mundo” por aquí, un “yo soy español” por allá y algún otro cántico que enseguida fue acallado por la potencia de los altavoces que empezaron a escupir unos ritmos de reggaeton a todo trapo.

Cerca de las 19.00 comenzó el show en Cibeles. Un animador que desprendía una energía que contagiaba al público, luego sesiones de Dj, para continuar con un breve concierto del grupo Viva Suecia y de Saiko antes de la llegada de los jugadores que antes de su visita al Palacio de la Zarzuela y al de Moncloa comenzaron su baño de masas en el aeropuerto, donde cientos de aficionados les esperaban, pero no tuvieron la suerte de poder verlos. Después de las visitas protocolarias llegó la fiesta en el autobús.

La multitud bulle a borbotones alrededor de Moncloa. Algo más alejados, aguardando a que llegue el autobús con los jugadores, una pareja espera en la hierba y a la sombra. A pesar de haber vivido las dos finales que ha vencido España, concuerdan en que la primera fue especial. “La alegría de aquel mundial fue mayor. Unió a todo el país. Consiguió que se levantaran todas las barreras entre nosotros, aunque luego acabara desdibujándose”, reflexiona Julián García, madrileño de 59 años. “Estoy feliz por el equipo maravilloso que se ha conseguido reunir, pero creo esta no nos va a unir tanto. No soy muy optimista. Hay demasiada polarización”, razona. “Pero habrá que ver”, concluye dejando el último aliento a la esperanza.

María Luisa Gómez, toledana de 62 años, espera a la rúa en la calle Princesa. Tiene en la muñeca una pulsera con la rojigualda y lleva gafas de sol. Lanza la misma idea: “Me ha encantado cómo esta selección juega en equipo, sin subrayar las genialidades y siendo el bien común lo que prima”, dice. “Ojalá se nos pegue como sociedad algo de lo que es este equipo”.

A los pocos minutos los gritos de “España, España, España” en la multitud alertan de que el autobús se aproxima. Más teléfonos arriba que bufandas al aire. “Vamos, España”, grita un niño con la camiseta del Barça y el nombre de Lamine Yamal. Ya están aquí. Los jugadores se sacan fotos con el público de fondo, levantan la copa y hasta se animan con el champán. Ferran, el goleador de la final, se lleva la gran parte de la atención. “¡Que Ferran ha lanzado un beso a una chica!”, comenta un grupo de adolescentes.

La rúa avanza y es difícil hacerse hueco. Pero en la esquina de la Glorieta de Ruiz Jiménez, Marisa Salmerón, de 90 años, lleva tiempo esperando acompañada de una nieta y dos hijas. Al principio aguarda expectante en la silla de ruedas hasta que el fervor anuncia la llegada de los jugadores. Entonces, se levanta, se apoya con el brazo izquierdo en la barandilla y con el brazo derecho saluda a toda la plantilla española. Tiene pintada en ambas mejillas la bandera rojigualda. Hace 16 años lo celebró en Cibeles con su marido, uno de los primeros socios del Real Madrid, cuenta orgullosa. Murió hace poco, a los 102 años. “Ojalá pudiera ver esto”, dice emocionada pero sin perder la sonrisa. “Estoy muy feliz”, alega.

En la calle de Sagasta, los gritos y vítores comienzan en cuanto el vehículo asoma por una recta que parecía infinita. Los jugadores han sido recibidos al grito de “campeones del mundo”. La multitud, cada vez más ansiosa, se anima entre bocinas y consignas.

Uno entre esa multitud es Jaime Tite, que tenía cuatro años cuando España ganó su primer Mundial. “Pero me acuerdo como si hubiera sido ayer. Teníamos la televisión cúbica esta”, recuerda. Ahora lo vive todo con más intensidad y mejor: rodeado de sus amigos, en la calle. “Ahora sí se puede sentir”.

Los jugadores llegaron a las 22.00 a Cibeles y con su llegada, la locura total. Júbilo entre los asistentes cuando Lamine Yamal y Nico Williams se pegaron sus bailecitos, cuando apareció Marcos Llorente con sus gafas, cuando Oyarzabal salió a escena con Potra Salvaje o cuando en última instancia apareció Rodri, el capitán. “Somos campeones del mundo. Viva la madre que nos parió”, dijo el MVP del Mundial. El centrocampista no quiso olvidarse del goleador de la final. “Me gustaría acordarme de una persona muy importante para mí, un jugador que ha sido injustamente criticado y que hoy es historia del fútbol español: Ferran”. Luego Borja Iglesias tomó los mandos de su mesa de mezclas para hacer de Dj y Aitana saltó al escenario con el público enloquecido para cantar la canción de España en el Mundial, Superestrella.

Una nueva generación ha nacido y con ella la ilusión de seguir conquistando el mundo.

World.title: El mal perder de Argentina: pelea tras la derrota y desplante a España durante la entrega de la Copa
World.content:
La permisividad del colegiado ante las reiteradas faltas de la Albiceleste marcó una final que derivó en una trifulca en la que Paredes agarró del cuello a Eric García

La final se fue endureciendo desde el primer minuto al compás de un arbitraje permisivo. Argentina, con un juego rudo y agresivo, convirtió el partido en un festival constante de patadas y faltas —una veintena por selección— sin que el esloveno Slavko Vinčić recurriera al bolsillo de las tarjetas hasta el minuto 40. La actuación del colegiado, que terminó con seis amarillas para la Albiceleste, la expulsión de Enzo Fernández y dos goles anulados a España en la prórroga, reavivó la polémica arbitral. Pero la tensión del encuentro no se esfumó tras el pitido final. Al contrario: acabó desbordándose.

Poco después de que el árbitro pitase el final del encuentro y España se proclamase campeona del mundo en Estados Unidos, varios futbolistas de Argentina provocaron enfrentamientos con los españoles que celebraban su segunda estrella sobre el césped del MetLife Stadium. Nahuel Molina golpeó a Rodri, Leandro Paredes agarró del cuello a Eric García y, junto a Thiago Almada, tiraron al suelo a Gavi cuando acudió a defender a su compañero, entre otras disputas. Aunque no fueron los únicos gestos que evidenciaron el mal perder de la Albiceleste tras el final del partido: los jugadores argentinos dieron la espalda al escenario en el que se producía la celebración de La Roja, y miraron a sus aficionados.

Hasta el minuto 40 no apareció la primera tarjeta del encuentro, tras una patada de Lisandro al borde de descanso para frenar a Oyarzabal. Y eso que antes ya se habían producido entradas duras, como la de Mac Allister sobre Dani Olmo o Tagliafico —repetidamente— sobre Lamine Yamal, y de las que salieron impunes.

Después, cinco amarillas más para la Albiceleste. Una de ellas precisamente para Paredes, que salió al inicio del segundo tiempo en lugar de Nico González, y tan solo necesitó siete minutos para ser amonestado tras una dura entrada sobre Rodri. Su juego agresivo no se detuvo, y continuó sumando faltas al límite de la expulsión.

Quien sí que vio la tarjeta roja fue Enzo Fernández en el descuento de la segunda mitad. El primer aviso le llegó en el minuto 82 por una protesta al árbitro esloveno Vinčić, y la segunda por una fuerte entrada contra Pau Cubarsí que hizo volar por los aires al central azulgrana, escogido mejor joven de todo el torneo. Mientras le atendían en el suelo, Messi buscaba al colegiado y pedía la expulsión de Cucurella por taparse la boca al hablar.

La entrada de Enzo Fernández contra Pau Cubarsí durante la final. DPA vía Europa Press (DPA vía Europa Press)

La prórroga solo hizo aumentar la tensión, con incluso Scaloni amonestado, y dos goles de La Roja anulados: uno por una falta sobre Otamendi y otra por fuera de juego. Con el tanto de Ferran y el pitido final, empezó una trifulca: Nahuel Molina golpeó a Rodri en el pecho mientras el capitán español corría a celebrar con sus compañeros la victoria de España. Cuando el centrocampista se dio la vuelta y se acercó a preguntarle el motivo de su puñetazo, Molina se encaró y ambos se empujaron. Eric lo vio, y se dirigió hacia el argentino rápidamente.

La pelea la agravó el centrocampista Paredes, que se encaró con Eric, primero tirándolo al suelo de un empujón, y luego agarrándole del cuello, desplazándolo hacia atrás. Gavi, que aún llevaba el peto de calentamiento, vio la escena, corrió y se lanzó sobre el centrocampista de Boca Juniors para defender a su compañero de equipo y selección, pero Paredes respondió tirando al azulgrana al suelo con la ayuda de Almada. Lamine Yamal rezaba de rodillas tranquilamente sobre el césped, ajeno a lo que sucedía detrás suyo, mientras integrantes de ambas selecciones acudían a separar a sus compañeros y evitaban que la situación escalase. Entre ellos, Borja Iglesias o el técnico argentino, Scaloni, que fue de los primeros en llegar para calmar las aguas.

Lendro Paredes y Thiago Armada empujan a Gavi, que cae al suelo tras el partido. Amanda Perobelli (REUTERS)

Pero su ayudante, Roberto Ayala, ya las había revuelto. Más en segundo plano de la trifulca, cámaras de los aficionados captaron cómo Ayala discutía con Dani Olmo y luego le propiciaba un puñetazo en la cara ante el desconcierto del español.

Hubo más encuentros verbales, con Otamendi encarándose con Rodri. “Empezá a hablar menos, boludo, que estuvisteis llorando toda la semana. Vos y Laporte. Eso no se hace. Estuvieron llorando con los árbitros, amigo”, le reprochó el argentino al capitán de la selección española ante la cara de asombro de este. “¿Qué he dicho?”, le preguntó Rodri, sorprendido, en una conversación que captaron las cámaras de Dazn.

Más tarde, mientras la selección española desfilaba para recoger las medallas y alzar la Copa del Mundo, los jugadores argentinos decidieron saltarse el protocolo y no presenciar la celebración de su rival: dieron la espalda a los españoles y miraron de frente a una de las gradas aún tintada de blanco y azul. Y así, Argentina cerró la final con una imagen lastimosa tan impropia como difícil de borrar.

World.title: La FIFA ya tiene los informes para investigar el comportamiento de Argentina en la final del Mundial y valorar posibles sanciones
World.content:
Señaló Slavko Vincic el final del partido en el MetLife Stadium de Nueva York y cuando todo parecía abocado a la celebración, a descorchar la tensión contenida durante los más de 120 minutos que duró la gran final de la Copa del Mundo, los jugadores de España se encontraron con un inesperado obstáculo: Nahuel Molina y Leandro Paredes, dos de los futbolistas que habían defendido sobre el césped los colores de la Albiceleste, mostraron comportamientos violentos contra algunos de los integrantes de la Selección.

El primero, lateral del Atlético de Madrid, golpeó a Rodri cuando el centrocampista madrileño del Manchester City corría a abrazar a sus compañeros sobre el terreno de juego. El segundo, con ficha en Boca Juniors, agredió primero a Eric García y después a Gavi, que había acudido raudo a la escena para defender a su compañero en la Roja y en el Barça. Molina y Paredes no fueron, sin embargo, los únicos en perder los estribos tras el desenlace del torneo, pues Roberto Fabián Ayala, exdefensor de Valencia y Zaragoza e integrante del cuerpo técnico de Lionel Scaloni, atacó a Dani Olmo pocos segundos después de que se desatara la trifulca.

La conducta de los argentinos no ha tardado en llegar a instancias de la FIFA. El órgano dirigido por Gianni Infantino ha nombrado a un inspector disciplinario para investigar el comportamiento de los futbolistas e integrantes de la Albiceleste y valorar posibles sanciones, según ha podido saber este periódico. Dicha figura, encargada de analizar las imágenes y tomar una decisión sobre las acciones de Molina, Paredes y Ayala, ya ha recibido los informes del colegiado de la final, el esloveno Slavko Vincic, y de los delegados de campo del partido. Atendiendo los precedentes, no obstante, el fallo de la FIFA todavía podría demorarse entre 15 y 20 días.

Nahuel Molina y Rodri se encaran tras el pitido final. Martin Rickett - PA Images (PA Images via Getty Images)

El precedente de Luis Suárez

No tardó tanto en conocerse —por la urgencia del calendario— la sanción a Luis Suárez, una de las más simbólicas y recientes en la Copa del Mundo. El 24 de junio de 2014, el delantero charrúa mordió a Giorgio Chiellini durante el Italia-Uruguay de la fase de grupos del Mundial de Brasil. Pese a las protestas del cuadro transalpino, el árbitro del encuentro, el mexicano Marco Rodríguez, no sancionó a Suárez sobre el césped (aún no existía el VAR).

La FIFA abrió un expediente disciplinario de oficio pocas horas después de que concluyera el encuentro y solo dos días más tarde, el 26 de junio de 2014, se apoyó en las imágenes de vídeo para imponer una de las sanciones más importantes que se recuerdan: nueve partidos de suspensión con la selección uruguaya, empezando por los octavos de final de ese mismo Mundial ante Colombia; cuatro meses de inhabilitación de cualquier actividad relacionada con el fútbol; y una multa económica de 82.000 euros.

Cierto es que, además de la dureza y la gravedad de la dentellada a Chiellini, la FIFA también apoyó entonces su decisión en la reincidencia de Suárez, que ya había mordido a un rival cuando militaba en las filas del Ajax, allá por 2010, y al serbio Branislav Ivanovic, del Chelsea, cuando defendía en 2013, solo un año antes de la Copa del Mundo, los colores del Liverpool.

La sanción, en cualquier caso, afectó al atacante uruguayo más allá de su rol con el combinado nacional. Ese mismo verano, Suárez fichó por el Barcelona, pero tuvo que esperar hasta el 25 de octubre, fecha del primer clásico liguero ante el Real Madrid, para estrenarse con la camiseta azulgrana en el Santiago Bernabéu, algo similar a lo que podría sucederle a los futbolistas argentinos investigados ahora por la FIFA por su conducta violenta ante España en Nueva York.

World.title: ¿Cómo ha ganado España el Mundial? Seis claves de su juego, fotograma a fotograma
World.content:
Analizamos paso a paso la superioridad en el centro del campo, las recuperaciones lejos del área o el gol que ha dado el título a la selección

España es campeona del mundo por segunda vez. Es la victoria de una forma de jugar que el equipo de Luis de la Fuente ha desplegado durante todo el torneo. Analizamos, fotograma a fotograma, las claves de su juego y el tanto que decidió la final.

1. Superioridad en el centro del campo

Durante toda la competición, Rodri, Pedri y Dani Olmo han combinado inteligencia táctica, capacidad para recuperar el balón y precisión para encontrar pases entre líneas. Esa superioridad en el centro del campo ha permitido a la selección controlar el ritmo de los partidos y acelerar en cuanto detecta un espacio.

Una de las mejores muestras de ello llegó en los octavos de final ante Portugal. Tras una pérdida del conjunto luso, Rodri recupera el balón y lo juega con Aymeric Laporte.

El balón llega a Pedri, que recibe de espaldas, gira sobre sí mismo y levanta la cabeza. En un solo movimiento identifica el hueco entre las líneas portuguesas y encuentra a Dani Olmo con un pase que rompe la primera línea defensiva. España va en tromba al ataque.

Olmo controla orientado y detecta el desmarque de Mikel Oyarzabal. Su pase filtrado supera a los centrales portugueses y deja al delantero lanzado a un mano a mano con Diogo Costa. Aunque no acaba en gol, la ocasión resume una de las grandes virtudes de España: convertir el dominio del centro en peligro inmediato.

2. La defensa: presión alta y recuperaciones

España ha construido su camino hasta la final desde la defensa. Con un solo gol encajado, la clave de su solidez defensiva ha sido recuperar el balón lejos de su portería. Según los datos de Driblab, ha sido el segundo equipo con mayor porcentaje de acciones defensivas en campo rival (62,5%), el que menos pases ha permitido completar a los delanteros rivales y el que menos ocasiones de gol ha concedido.

Una jugada ante Austria resume bien cómo ha funcionado la presión tras pérdida. En el minuto 73, Ferran Torres pierde un balón en campo rival tras una conducción. El centrocampista Florian Grillitsch lo recupera y juega hacia atrás, pero Mikel Merino, Lamine Yamal y el propio Ferran saltan a la presión en la frontal del área, mientras Oyarzabal adelanta su posición para cerrar las líneas de pase. Austria no encuentra salida y acaba perdiendo de nuevo la posesión.

La misma secuencia se repitió en los octavos frente a Portugal. Pedro Neto recibe presionado por Marc Cucurella y un control defectuoso permite a Álex Baena recuperar el balón. En apenas unos segundos, España transforma una acción defensiva en una ocasión de peligro: Baena filtra el pase hacia Rodri y la selección vuelve a instalarse en el área contraria.

Incluso cuando ha estado por delante en el marcador, España ha seguido presionando la salida rival. A tres minutos del final del partido contra Bélgica (2-1), tras un saque de banda, Mikel Merino persigue al portero mientras Ferran Torres tapa el pase hacia el defensa. Sin opciones en corto, el guardameta se ve obligado a jugar en largo y España recupera el balón.

3. La profundidad de los laterales

La profundidad y explosividad por las bandas son un sello distintivo de España desde la Eurocopa de 2024. Entonces fue la amplitud de Lamine Yamal y de Nico Williams; esta vez fueron Pedro Porro y Marc Cucurella. Porro ha sido el principal generador de peligro desde los costados: suyo ha sido incluso el centro que generó el gol de la final. Y Cucurella ha sido uno de los laterales con más precisión de pases, según datos de Driblab.

Una jugada del partido de dieciseisavos ante Austria resume bien el papel de los laterales en el ataque de España. Después de que un defensa bloquea un disparo de Dani Olmo, el balón cae a los pies de Marc Cucurella en la frontal del área. Al otro lado del campo, Pedro Porro ha acompañado la acción y avanza prácticamente a la misma altura.

Tras imponerse en el duelo con un defensa austríaco, Cucurella abre el juego hacia Álex Baena.

El extremo controla el balón junto a la línea de fondo y espera el momento adecuado para poner el centro, una pausa que permite a Porro incorporarse al área sin oposición.

Porro irrumpe libre hasta la altura del punto de penalti y remata de cabeza con potencia para firmar el 2-0. La imagen que deja la jugada resume el funcionamiento de España: la acción termina con sus dos laterales dentro del área adversaria.

4. Los cambios que funcionan

El banquillo también ha sido decisivo en el recorrido hasta la final. La mejor muestra llegó en los octavos de final ante Portugal, un partido que se resolvió en el minuto 90 con un gol construido por tres futbolistas que habían entrado desde el banquillo: Ferran Torres, Fabián Ruiz y Mikel Merino.

La jugada nace de una falta sobre Merino en campo portugués. En lugar de detenerse, el centrocampista se levanta de inmediato y pone el balón en juego hacia Fabián Ruiz, sorprendiendo a una defensa que aún no ha terminado de reorganizarse.

Fabián descarga de primeras para Rodri, que, también al primer toque, encuentra a Ferran Torres con un pase vertical que rompe la presión y supera varias líneas de Portugal.

Ferran controla, fija a los centrales con apenas un par de toques y espera el instante preciso. Ese breve retraso permite que Merino ataque el espacio a la espalda de Rúben Dias y aparezca completamente liberado.

El pase de Ferran deja a Merino frente a Diogo Costa. El centrocampista orienta su carrera sin necesidad de tocar el balón y, ante la salida del portero, define con un disparo al primer palo siguiendo la trayectoria del envío.

Esta acción resuelta por los suplentes no fue un caso aislado. En los cuartos de final ante Bélgica, España volvió a encontrar la solución en el banquillo: Mikel Merino, que también había arrancado como suplente, marcó el gol decisivo en los minutos finales para sellar el pase a semifinales.

5. La jugada perfecta

El segundo gol ante Francia, en semifinales, condensó en apenas un minuto muchas de las señas de identidad de la España de Luis de la Fuente. La jugada nace de una presión coordinada sobre la salida de balón, continúa con una larga secuencia de pases y movimientos sin balón y termina con Pedro Porro, un lateral, definiendo dentro del área tras una combinación al primer toque.

Todo empieza un minuto antes del remate, cuando España presiona la salida del portero francés. Dani Olmo salta sobre el guardameta mientras Lamine Yamal, Fabián Ruiz y Mikel Oyarzabal cierran las líneas de pase más cercanas. Sin opciones para jugar en corto, el meta se ve obligado a enviar un balón largo.

España recupera inmediatamente la posesión y mueve la pelota con paciencia entre Unai Simón, Laporte, Rodri, Fabián Ruiz y Pedro Porro, hasta volver a encontrar a Rodri. En ese intercambio, Porro abandona el carril derecho para aparecer por dentro y generar superioridad en la zona de creación, mientras Dani Olmo rompe a la espalda de Manu Koné en busca de un espacio entre líneas.

El desenlace llega con una combinación de manual. Porro filtra un pase hacia Olmo y continúa su carrera. El delantero devuelve el balón al primer toque, dejando al lateral lanzado hacia el área. La defensa francesa pierde las referencias: ni Koné ni Doué acompañan el desmarque de Porro y Lacroix sale a cubrir a Oyarzabal, abriendo un pasillo decisivo.

Porro controla y define con precisión para culminar una acción que resume el estilo de España. La selección desactivó el ataque más productivo del Mundial a partir de sus propias fortalezas: una presión colectiva, una circulación paciente pero vertical, la movilidad constante de sus futbolistas y la capacidad de sus laterales para aparecer donde menos los espera el rival.

6. Cuatro toques para el gol del Mundial

Recién empezado el segundo tiempo de la prórroga de la final, España sigue con su asedio a Argentina, que ya juega con uno menos. En el minuto 105 arranca una jugada en la que intervienen los cambios —tres de los protagonistas— y las dos bandas.

Zubimendi, que entró por Rodri en el minuto 99, abre hacia Lamine Yamal, que, presionado por dos jugadores argentinos, descarga hacia atrás para Pedro Porro.

Porro centra de primera, sin parar el balón. Antes de que salga el envío, Nico Williams ya corre hacia el segundo palo.

Nico, marcado por Molina, alcanza el balón y consigue cabecear directamente hacia el centro del área. En el siguiente fotograma se aprecia cómo hacia allí se dirige Ferran, completamente solo: tres defensas argentinos han seguido a Mikel Merino, más cerca de la portería, y Giuliano Simeone, al borde del área, ni amaga con perseguir al delantero español.

Ferran no para el balón y saca un disparo perfecto con la zurda, por encima de Dibu Martínez y de los defensas. Desde Lamine hasta él solo ha habido cuatro toques: Porro, Nico Williams y Ferran lo han hecho todo de primera.

World.title: De Keyne, el hermano de Lamine Yamal, a la familia numerosa de Cucurella: los apoyos de los jugadores de la selección española fuera del campo
World.content:
Quien también estuvo acompañado de su familia fue Nico Williams. El jugador vasco, que dio la asistencia de la victoria, posó junto a familiares y amigos en el terreno de juego. "He pisado mierda, he comido mierda y ahora estoy besando el santo. Es el día más feliz de mi vida", aseguró Williams tras la victoria de España. Y en ese momento de plenitud, también quiso hacer partícipe a su madre del hito conseguido. María Arthuer, presente en la grada junto a otros familiares, recibió el mejor de los regalos: su hijo acudió hasta su lugar para entregarle la medalla de campeón. Los padres de Nico Williams y del también jugador Iñaki Williams se embarcaron hace 30 años en un viaje largo y peligroso. Abandonaron su país natal, Ghana, y llegaron hasta Navarra, donde nacieron sus dos hijos. "Nos transmitieron siempre humildad, ese es el pilar de nuestra familia, somos así en todo y afrontamos las cosas desde esa manera de ver el mundo con valentía y mucho trabajo", afirmó el campeón del mundo en una entrevista con 'El País Semanal' en 2024. Y añadió: "Nuestro caso representa bien lo que supone ese viaje de la inmigración. Lo que conlleva de adaptación y aceptación. Podemos ser una voz que abra puertas al futuro".

Hector Vivas - FIFA (FIFA via Getty Images)
