World.title: Tweed hospital redevelopment to deliver 800 new homes
World.content:
A northern New South Wales mayor has welcomed the decision to increase the density of an large apartment complex at Tweed Heads, but has urged the state government to increase the amount of affordable housing in the complex.

The NSW government this week unveiled a master plan for the redevelopment the former Tweed Hospital site, creating 800 high-density units.

Meanwhile, housing density at the East Lismore housing development on land formerly owned by Southern Cross University has also increased from 400 to 500 homes.

The Minister for the North Coast, Janelle Saffin said Tweed Heads had a "dire need" for housing, with a vacancy rate of 0.8 per cent.

"Tweed Heads is one of the fastest-growing communities in NSW, which has placed immense pressure on local rental and housing markets," she said.

Tweed Mayor Chris Cherry welcomed the creation of more homes but said the state government could do better than allocating just 10 per cent of the development as affordable housing.

The former Tweed hospital site will be transformed into 800 new homes. (Supplied: NSW government)

"We certainly welcome this commitment by the state government to get housing onto that site. It's prime real estate in Tweed Heads, so to get a residential outcome is a great one," Cr Cherry said.

"It's ideal for affordable housing and getting some of that low-cost, key-worker housing that we really need in the shire.

"I'm hoping, because it's a public piece of land that the community already owns, that maybe we could get something a bit higher than that in terms of affordable housing," she said.

" Eighty units will help, but more is always better. "

The old hospital site is prime waterfront real estate. (ABC North Coast: Elloise Farrow-Smith)

Affordable housing 'negative' value

Landcom's executive general manager of the built form division, Andrew Cooper, said planning was still in the early stages, but confirmed at least 10 per cent of the development would be affordable housing.

Mr Cooper said there needed to be a mix of affordable and market value housing to make the development viable.

"Unfortunately, affordable housing has negative land value,. That's just the nature of the costs in 2026. You need the market housing to effectively support the affordable housing," he said.

Andrew Cooper says Landcom is committed to a component of affordable housing within their developments. (ABC North Coast: Cath Adams)

Teresa Mitchell, the founding director and CEO of AGAPE Outreach, was disappointed there was no social housing included in the development.

"The fact that there's no social housing is kind of sad. We've got sole parent pensioners, we've got people on disability payments, we've got youth, so not having any social housing is just not going to cater for any of these people.

"There are so many in this area in need of housing. We need housing, we really do. But, it's just not going to cater for the people who live here."

Homeless people living in tents in the banks of the Tweed River. (ABC North Coast: Elloise Farrow-Smith)

The State Significant Development Application for the Tweed Heads development will be lodged in early 2027 with construction expected to commence in 2029, pending planning approvals.

Meanwhile, the construction of 50 rent-to-buy units in East Lismore by Landcom was on-track for occupation by February, Mr Cooper said.

Next door, the state government has added an extra 100 homes to the 400-lot being developed by Landcom as part of the Reconstruction Authority's Resilient Lands Program.

Funding will also be provided to support infrastructure upgrades, such as water and sewerage, as required.

The first lots will be available for people relocating from homes bought back by the Reconstruction Authority as part of the Resilient Homes Program.

The retail sale of around 100 lots was expected to begin in October, and will be released over five years.

World.title: Police investigate stabbing of 15-year-old in Melbourne's south-east
World.content:
Police are investigating after a high school student was stabbed in Melbourne's south-east on Monday afternoon.

A 15-year-old boy was found with serious injuries after an altercation between a group of teenagers, Victoria Police said.

Ambulance Victoria said paramedics responded to reports of an incident in Cranbourne North at around 3:20pm, where they treated one patient.

"A teenage boy was transported by road ambulance to hospital with upper body injuries in a serious condition," a spokesperson said.

Police said the group of teenagers fled the scene on foot.

The Department of Education said the injured teenager was a student of Alkira Secondary College but that the assault took place "outside the school and after school hours".

"The college is providing wellbeing support to those involved," a department spokesperson said.

The ABC understands the alleged offender is not an Alkira Secondary College student.

Anyone who witnessed the incident, has dashcam or CCTV footage or information is urged to contact Crime Stoppers.

World.title: Nicaragua's president extends rule, says country will not hold elections soon
World.content:
Nicaragua's President Daniel Ortega says his country will not hold elections anytime soon.

The statement underscores the strongman's efforts to extend his nearly 20-year rule and dashes hopes by the opposition that he might heed their demands for a democratic vote.

The announcement also effectively cancelled Nicaragua's next elections, originally scheduled for November 2027.

In January 2025 its government-controlled congress voted to extend the five-year presidential term by one year.

Mr Ortega spoke at the anniversary of the Sandinista Revolution that toppled the Somoza dictatorship in 1979 and first brought him to power.

He returned to the presidency in 2007 and has since rewritten the constitution, crushed political opposition and solidified his control over virtually all branches of the Nicaraguan government.

Nicaragua political turmoil as president detains rivals President Daniel Ortega is leaving nothing to chance ahead of presidential elections later this year

Since mass protests in 2018, which led to a bloody government crackdown that killed hundreds, Mr Ortega and his wife and co-President Rosario Murillo have been holding on to power.

Mr Ortega declared himself the winner of the 2021 election in a vote widely viewed as illegitimate by the international community and after jailing all the candidates who could have possibly beaten him.

"There won't be anymore elections," Mr Ortega said in a speech railing against his longtime adversary, the United States.

"Parties put in place by the Yankees, put in place by the Somoza regime, coming back to power — that story is over.

"Never, never, never," he said of any future elections.

Daniel Ortega has rewritten the constitution, crushed political opposition and solidified control over the government. (Reuters: Leonardo Fernandez Viloria, file )

Opponents say nation moving to one-party rule

Opponents and rights groups said the announcement represented an escalation as Mr Ortega further solidified his grip on Nicaragua.

Juan Sebastián Chamorro, a 2021 candidate who was behind bars until he was released to the US in 2023 with more than 200 other political prisoners, said the announcement revealed Mr Ortega's longstanding plan to consolidate power in the hands of the Sandinista party, similar to other one-party rule countries like China and Cuba.

"Ortega and Murillo are evidently afraid at the idea that the slightest political opening could create the conditions for dissent to manifest and threaten their grip on power," said Tiziano Breda, a senior Latin America analyst at independent conflict monitor ACLED.

"Instead of staging a rigged election, they have opted to eliminate electoral competition altogether," he added.

Danny Ramírez Ayérdiz, a Nicaraguan lawyer and founder of the Interamerican Center for Legal Assistance in Human Rights, which investigates abuses of the Ortega-Murillo government from Argentina, said the announcement "reveals the face of a dictatorship that, without any shame, has entrenched itself in power".

"It indicates a potentially higher level of repression against people who demand the removal of the government or the holding of elections," Mr Ramírez Ayérdiz said.

Castro's daughter hopes US can change Cuba Fidel Castro's daughter says the US has failed to find a way to deal with Cuba for decades. But she tells the ABC that the Trump administration has a difference that could spell the end of the regime she fled.

At least 46 people are behind bars in Nicaragua for political reasons, according to the Mechanism for Recognition of Political Prisoners group, which tracks the cases.

Nicaragua denies holding political prisoners.

In the wake of the US military operation that captured Venezuela's then-president Nicolás Maduro in a January raid, the Nicaraguan government said it would release more prisoners, apparently in an effort to stave off pressure on itself.

But there has been no follow-up and little transparency on the issue.

At least one imprisoned activist has died since then.

Since 2018, Nicaragua has also shuttered more than 5,000 organisations, largely religious, and forced thousands to flee the country.

Earlier in July, the Ortega-Murillo government stripped masses of lawyers of their licences to practise in what UN experts called a "purge of the legal profession".

AP

World.title: Ian doesn't want children. He's part of a growing trend among men
World.content:
Ian was 13 when his dad moved out. He says it was about then he first thought having kids wasn't for him.

"I was probably destined not to have them based on what I know about the males in my family," the 48-year-old from Adelaide/Tarntanya says.

"I didn't want to repeat my dad's mistakes."

Ian considers himself a "wanderer". He says his desire to "drift through the world a bit" means he didn't think fatherhood was an ideal fit.

About 15 per cent of Australian men say they don't want children, according to the 2025 Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) survey.

That's up from 11 per cent in 2005.

Much of the research into the decision to be childfree, or voluntarily childless, has focused on women. Researchers say that is no surprise "since having children is more strongly socially prescribed for women" and women bear "greater costs and risks to having a child than men".

Imogene Smith, a clinical psychologist and lecture at The Cairnmillar Institute, is one of few Australian researchers who has studied child-free men.

She says talking about why men are turning way from fatherhood can help them feel supported in their decision.

Why more men are choosing not to have children

Family of origin was a common reason men shared for not wanting children in Dr Smith's surveys.

The difference between childfree and childless While not everyone in the childless or childfree communities will identify the same way, understanding the difference means we can respond more thoughtfully when learning about someone's parental status.

"[Fatherhood] didn't sound appealing to them," Dr Smith says.

Some touched on the relationship with their father "turning them away" from parenting, or having lots of siblings and seeing how hard it was for their parents, for example.

"It wasn't always a dad thing, but it was something to do with that template of what we all have in our mind of what it looks like to be a parent, which is firmly rooted in our parents," Dr Smith says.

She says for some, there was a desire to be "alternative".

"We had a fair bit of 'I'm different, I don't see myself in that way ... not wanting to follow the norm."

There were men who had felt firm in their decision from when they were young, says Dr Smith.

Participants also talked about various fears. For example, concerns about the climate or political environment, or passing on inheritable conditions around mental and physical health.

And despite Dr Smith's sample of men largely being middle class and professionals, a lot had financial concerns.

"They just couldn't see how they could afford a bigger house to have a kid," she says.

Are you a man who has chosen not to have children? We'd love to hear from you about why

Men were also influenced by the experience of raising children they saw around them, like their friends with kids, or watching parents at a cafe.

"A lot of uncles saying, 'Nope, I have seen my brother, and he has no free time'.

"One man said something about it ruining his sex life. He said, 'My friends who've got two kids, they have Dora the Explorer sex … however long that episode is, that's how long they've got to do it.'"

Do men face societal pressure to have kids?

While Ian knew in his teens that he didn't want kids, he says he gave himself permission to change his mind.

" I kept an open mind that whole time, if I changed my mind, I am allowed to change my mind. "

But that never happened. Ian met his wife, who "was of the same mindset" 16 years ago.

Their desire to stay childfree is part of what pulled them together, he says.

Ian says he's content with being a dog owner. (Supplied)

Child-free men have previously shared with ABC Lifestyle experiencing a pressure to carry on the family name, or judgement that they are not a "real man" if they don't have kids.

Dr Smith says most of the men she spoke with said any societal pressure they faced "just washes over" them.

"They just kind of laughed [when I asked about it] — they just weren't bothered."

Previous research has shown that childless men have poorer health outcomes, are at higher risk of social disconnection, and face negative stigma. But Dr Smith suspects that could be because much of the research focuses on older men of previous generations.

"If you waited until the current generation of 30-year-olds was 70 or 80, you might get a different result."

How child-free men are viewed by others

While Ian hasn't felt pressure to have children, he says his child-free status does raise eyebrows when meeting new people.

"Someone [at work] asked me just the other day 'Have you got kids? You don't ever do the school run?' I said 'I don't have kids' and they were shocked."

Tom Denson, a professor in the School of Psychology at UNSW, co-authored research published earlier this year looking at the negative bias child-free people experience.

It found child-free men experience less bias than child-free women for making the same choice not to have children.

"Child-free men were rated higher in interpersonal warmth than child-free women, who were viewed as less warm," Professor Denson says.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

A study into the stigma and societal pressures for voluntary childless men and women found women are seen by society as "spinsters", while men were "living the dream".

Dr Smith says the men in her study "weren't overly concerned" about people judging them for their choice.

"They went to the effort of telling me, unprompted, what they do to contribute to society and leave their own kind of legacy.

"Some of them men were telling me about their charity work, places they donate to, some worked with young people.

"They felt quite OK about contributing to society in their own way. And had a strong sense of this choice doesn't make me less than somebody who has a child."

World.title: India steps up response to US, Iran deadly ship strikes
World.content:
Samar Chaurasia used to speak to his father, Shivanand Chaurasia, on the phone several times a day while he worked overseas on an oil tanker. Then, without warning, the calls stopped.

Shivanand Chaurasia, an engine fitter just six months into his first voyage, was among three crew members killed on June 10, when MT Settebello was struck in the Gulf of Oman during an attack by the United States.

Since the US-Israel war with Iran began, 10 Indian sailors have been killed and dozens more injured — some critically — as commercial cargo ships and oil tankers have repeatedly come under attack in the battle for control of key shipping lanes in the Middle East.

Seafarers 'pay the price' in the war in Iran Three Indian sailors have been killed in a US military operation in the Strait of Hormuz.

Indians make up one of the world's largest merchant shipping workforces, with more than 300,000 seafarers employed globally, according to Indian government data.

The US alleged the ship Samar's father was on was carrying sanctioned Iranian oil, but the vessel operator denied it was associated with Tehran and said no warning was issued before the ship was struck.

India's government has now become one of the first to take action to try and protect its sailors, including new monitoring measures and asking companies to stop hiring Indian workers.

But for some families, the measures have come too late.

'My brother did nothing wrong'

Shivanand Chaurasia was the sole earner for his family.

His wife, Sushila, said the family sold their farmland to pay for his training to become an engine fitter.

Sushila has been left devastated by the loss of her husband. (ABC News: Som Patidar)

"My entire world collapsed when I heard the news," the 31-year-old said.

"He loved our children very much; he loved me very much. He couldn't go a single day without speaking to us.

"He used to call at least four times a day."

Samar's father was trying to save up to send him to a better school. (ABC News: Rachel Clayton )

Sushila said the last call she had with her husband was at 9pm the night before the oil tanker he was working on was attacked.

"I was at my mother's house. He asked how we were, and I told him to call back in five minutes because our youngest was crying," she said.

"That's the last time I spoke to him."

Sushila said her family has asked for 1 crore ($148,500) in compensation from the Indian government to help support her two children: six-year-old Samar and two-year-old Vyamika.

"He was on the ship for six months, and we didn't get a single penny sent home," she said.

Vyamika Chaurasia lost her father while he was overseas. (ABC News: Rachel Clayton)

Sushila, like other Indian families who have lost loved ones to the war, struggled to understand why Indians are being dragged into a conflict they want nothing to do with.

"I want to tell America: Why are you killing Indians even though they have nothing to do with war?" she said.

"If ships are not allowed, seafarers are not allowed there; then please send them back home. Do not kill them."

Shivanand's younger brother Ram Pravesh echoed her anger.

Ram Pravesh Chaurasia says his brother was killed while simply trying to earn money. (ABC News: Som Patidar)

"This is a fight between Iran and Israel and America … but it's Indians who are being hit," he said.

"My brother did nothing wrong. He went there to work, to earn money, and they killed him."

Shipping companies warned not to hire Indians

As the killing of Indian workers continues, the Indian government has been forced to take action.

Last week, two separate ship attacks killed engineer Herambh Karmark and engine officer Rohan Kumar, which the US blamed on Iran.

Three crew members were killed in the US attack on the Palau-flagged tanker MT Settebello. (Reuters: Priyanshu Singh)

In the wake of the two deaths, New Delhi lodged a strong protest with Iran, summoning its deputy ambassador over the recent deaths of its seafarers and announced a series of new measures.

India's Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways will now actively begin monitoring every Indian seafarer on every vessel in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, and the Gulf of Oman using a real-time dashboard to be built by the country's Directorate General of Shipping.

The government has not said how it will collect the data, particularly if a ship's transponder is turned off.

It also issued an advisory notice to shipping companies to avoid hiring any new Indian workers for voyages through the Strait of Hormuz.

The notice makes shipping companies responsible if newly hired Indian crew members are injured or killed.

Yet unions have demanded even stronger action, given 20,000 sailors remain on board 1,600 commercial vessels in or around the Strait of Hormuz.

The Maritime Union of India has asked members to sign a petition addressed to Prime Minister Narendra Modi demanding he use diplomacy to "secure safe passage, de-escalation, and humanitarian protection" for all workers in the Strait of Hormuz.

The Forward Seamen's Union of India (FSUI) has also urged Mr Modi "to register a strict official protest with the [United Nations] against the killing of innocent Indian seafarers in the US-Israel-Iran conflict zone".

"Dozens of Indian lives have been lost due to targeted attacks on civilian merchant ships. Seafarers are not collateral damage," the union said in a statement on X.

The FSUI is also demanding an immediate, independent inquiry into the deadly strikes, compensation of $US5 million ($7.13 million) for the families of those killed, and stronger safety protocols to protect maritime workers who remain in the region.

'No compensation' despite risky deployment

Rescued sailors contacted by the ABC have said they cannot talk about what happened because it could jeopardise their chances of being hired again.

The tankers that reignited the war The commercial tankers struck as they transited the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks were "highly, highly targeted", according to marine traffic watchers.

But the older brother of a sailor who survived the attack on the MT Settebello said his sibling described being stranded on the ship after the strike took out the ship's power.

"He was completely shaken for the first 10 days after he returned," the man, who the ABC has chosen not to identify, said.

He said his brother still gets frightened if he hears loud bangs.

" There's been no compensation from the company for being involved in such a risky deployment. "

The sailor's brother said most ships' crews were aware that attacks from Iran or the US almost always targeted the engine room, and if they had had prior warning, they would have made sure that room had been cleared.

"They did not have any information about the attack. Otherwise, the chief engineer and fitter would not have been in the engine room."

World.title: Diplomatic efforts to keep US from cutting ties with UNHCR begin, sources say
World.content:
As the Trump administration continues to weigh up cutting ties with the UN refugee agency (UNHCR), a campaign by diplomats and UN officials to persuade the United States to maintain support has begun.

Eight sources including diplomats, aid sources and a congressional source have told Reuters that Washington, historically UNHCR's largest donor, has been considering disengaging from the agency.

Several said a decision had been expected last week, but no announcement was made, suggesting the lobbying effort may have helped delay or avert a move.

Reuters granted the sources anonymity to speak about UN relations with the US.

The US deliberations over leaving UNHCR, which was created in the aftermath of World War II to help refugees fleeing war, persecution and violence, follow a disagreement over the appointment of the deputy high commissioner, five of the sources said.

They said the agency had informed supporters it could be placed on a US blacklist, ending funding, and Washington could also withdraw from its governing executive committee.

Any end to US funding would seriously weaken the agency at a time of near-record levels of displacement around the world amid long-running conflicts like Ukraine and Sudan, diplomats and aid officials said.

The US was the top donor to UNHCR in 2025. (Reuters: Saul Loeb)

"People have been alerted by UNHCR to call friends in the administration," a source at an aid group involved in the talks told Reuters, saying many had done so.

"They are at least thinking about it," the source said.

Another diplomat said UNHCR officials had asked supporters in the past week to use all available diplomatic channels with the United States to urge ongoing support.

A UN refugee agency spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

"We have no comment on this issue because we have no information on it," UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said.

A State Department spokesperson said there have not been any changes to Washington's engagement with UNHCR.

How US exit from WHO will impact global health Global health experts fear Donald Trump's plan to withdraw the US from the World Health Organization could roll back decades-long gains made in fighting diseases and increase pandemic risks.

"As with many other international organisations, we work with and through UNHCR when doing so is useful to advance US foreign policy interests or save lives," the spokesperson said.

"We will continue to evaluate the United States's role in international organisations," they said, referring to a February 2025 executive order to review US participation and funding.

Since beginning his second term last year, President Donald Trump has cut funding for UN agencies and withdrawn from dozens of UN entities including the World Health Organization.

Trump officials have also urged other nations to join a global campaign to roll back asylum protections.

Leadership dilemma

The dispute centres on last month's appointment of US career diplomat Tressa Rae Finerty as UNHCR's deputy high commissioner.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and UN High Commissioner for Refugees Barham Salih chose Ms Finerty over Simon Hankinson, a US-backed candidate and former foreign service officer who has accused the UNHCR of pursuing "a mass migration agenda".

"If they wanted reform, a return to UNHCR's original mission of helping actual refugees, and a careful inspection of budgets and spending, I was the guy," he told Reuters, calling Ms Finerty a "business as usual" candidate.

Reuters could not reach Ms Finerty for comment.

A former senior UNHCR official said Mr Salih, a former Iraqi president and refugee, would have faced internal "uproar" had he backed Mr Hankinson.

Other UN agencies like the International Labour Organization have also faced dilemmas over appointing US officials amid questions about the US commitment to global cooperation.

Andrew Veprek, Assistant Secretary of State in the Bureau of Population, Refugees and Migration who has espoused anti-migration views, was involved in backing Mr Hankinson's candidacy, two of the sources said.

The US State Department declined to comment on his involvement.

UNHCR works across 122 countries, including in Chad. (Reuters: Amr Abdallah Dalsh/File)

Top donor

The US was the top donor to UNHCR in 2025, giving $868 million or about a quarter of the total contributions, according to the agency.

UNHCR is already facing a financial crisis after available funding fell about 30 per cent in 2025 compared with 2024, Reuters reported.

The agency has cut thousands of jobs and announced further cuts this year.

Diplomats and aid officials said a full US withdrawal would deepen the crisis and undermine support for the 1951 Refugee Convention, the cornerstone of the post-war refugee protection system.

"Rethinking it would be an existential threat for UNHCR," the former UNHCR official said.

"It could have a massive knock-on effect."

Reuters

World.title: 'Don't go there': Pauline Hanson fires up in Q&A over White Australia policy
World.content:
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has angrily denied suggestions her strident opposition to migration by anyone from "radical Islamic countries" amounts to a version of the White Australia policy.

Ms Hanson was speaking at a Perth leadership breakfast hosted by The West Australian newspaper, after returning from the UK where she had blamed the end of the White Australia policy for migration issues in Australia during an interview with far-right activist and convicted criminal Tommy Robinson.

During a question-and-answer session at this morning's event, Senator Hanson spoke about radicalisation and terrorism carried out by Muslims, namely last year's Bondi terror attack.

"You've got to call out the elephant in the room," she said.

"And I'm sorry to say this but I don't want people coming to this country from radical Islamic countries.

Pauline Hanson addresses the Leadership Matters event at Crown Perth. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"I don't want that here. I want to protect the Australian people, I want them to feel safe in the streets. I don't want to see this anti-Semitism that's going on. I don't want to see the hatred that's happening.

"That's why I'm very strong on certain countries. You've got to say no."

'Nothing to do' with White Australia policy

Challenged by the event's host on whether this was a version of the White Australia policy, Senator Hanson strongly rejected the suggestion.

"No, it's not,' she said.

"It's got nothing to do with that. It's got nothing to do with the White Australia policy at all. So don't go there with me, I tell you what, because I won't stand for it."

She said she had never supported the White Australia policy.

In a wide-ranging address to the event, Senator Hanson lauded Western Australia's small business community and said the state helped "pay this nation's bills", while generating a huge portion of business investment.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson took part in a question and answer session after addressing the event. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

But she noted it also had an extremely low rental vacancy rate and again sought to blame migration.

Perth visit follows UK trip

Senator Hanson has just returned from a visit to Europe and the UK, where she spoke at a conservative conference and took part in the controversial interview with Robinson.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson gave a speech in London on the weekend. (ABC News: Riley Stuart)

In her address to the business breakfast, Senator Hanson addressed the media attention she had received for meeting Robinson, saying: "I sat down with a lot of people, some I agree with, some I don't".

"But Australians are sick of politicians who only ever talk to people who already agree with them.

"I went to Britain to see up close what happens when a government gets things wrong. Immigration. Spending. Energy."

Senator Hanson was asked by the event host who would be paying for her trip to Europe, where she was pictured at a luxury villa in Sicily with mining magnate Gina Rinehart and attended a fashion party.

"It didn't cost the taxpayer one cent for my trip overseas. Not one cent," she said.

Hanson risks losing everyday Australians while busy with the richest Many voters are unhappy with the hand they feel successive governments have dealt them and no-one has tapped into that better than Pauline Hanson.

She was not pressed further on the issue but added no one's private life was questioned like hers.

With One Nation polling strongly, Senator Hanson said she "had no doubt" she could do the job of prime minister.

"It's not about Pauline Hanson becoming prime minister. I want the right person in the right job. And if someone I believe can do a better job than I can, then go for it."

Quizzed on whether high-profile One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce could be that person, she said she had not discussed that with him but Mr Joyce, a former deputy prime minister, had the experience.

One Nation eyes WA by-election

During a media conference after the event, Senator Hanson said no deal had been struck with the WA Liberals on preferences for an upcoming state by-election in Perth's far southern suburbs.

But WA Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas has said he was open to finding a way to work with One Nation, and Ms Hanson told reporters she would "definitely" like to work with Zempilas.

Meet the candidates in the Secret Harbour by-election Here's everything you need to know about the Secret Harbour by-election, which is shaping up as one of the most closely-watched political contests in WA for some time.

One Nation's candidate in the poll Luke Herdegen was asked about a 2019 social media post where he admitted heavily using cocaine and how he had changed his life since.

"That's a story I put out there to try and help inspire people to live happier and healthier lives and I think it really did help a lot of people," Mr Herdegen said.

"When I'm in the streets of Secret Harbour they're not asking me about a blog post from 10 years ago."

One Nation candidate for Secret Harbour Luke Herdegen answers questions from media on Tuesday. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

On the weekend, One Nation state MP Rod Caddies was vaunting the thoroughness of the party's candidate vetting process.

But when Senator Hanson was questioned about Mr Herdegen's cocaine use earlier in the media conference, she said she did not know anything about it.

"I have been out of the country and I just briefly met Luke yesterday," she said.

Protesters rally outside

Around 80 protesters gathered outside Crown Perth ahead of the event.

Around 80 protesters gathered outside Crown Perth on Tuesday. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

The protest, organised by the WA Socialists and the WA Greens, was positioned at the entrance to the venue with protesters chanting at cars as they entered.

Protesters held signs with Ms Hanson's face on it and chanted phrases such as "migrants are welcome, racists are not" and "Seven West you can't hide", referring to The West Australian's owner.

Mining magnate Gina Rinehart, a powerful supporter of Hanson, has a 9.15 per cent interest in Seven West's parent company Southern Cross Media via an investment made by her Hancock Prospecting company.

There was a heavy police presence at the protest with around 17 officers positioned around the group, as well as police horses.

Around 80 protesters gathered outside Crown Perth ahead of the event. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Senator Hanson yesterday visited the electorate of Secret Harbour, south of Perth, where a state by-election will be held on August 29.

She was seen speaking to people in Secret Harbour alongside One Nation candidate Luke Herdegen, a gym owner and former champion weightlifter.

It is the second time Senator Hanson has travelled to Western Australia in as many months.

World.title: Weatherald retains Australian Test spot despite middling Ashes returns
World.content:
Opening batsman Jake Weatherald has retained his spot in Australia's Test squad for the looming series against Bangladesh.

Despite a middling Ashes campaign last summer, Weatherald is among a 13-man squad bolstered by the return of a trio of big guns.

Captain Pat Cummins, paceman Josh Hazlewood and spinner Nathan Lyon all return after recovering from injury.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"They have worked extremely hard, individually and with the [fitness] teams, over the past few months to return from their respective injuries," Australia's chairman of selectors George Bailey said.

"While this is a 13-player squad, we have players prepared and available should any adjustments be required in the lead-up to these matches.

"The volume of cricket and schedule across the next 12 months are likely to present further opportunities across all formats for many players."

Missing from Australia's squad for the final Test against England last January are Usman Khawaja (retired), Michael Neser, Todd Murphy and Brendan Doggett.

The Australians host Bangladesh in Darwin from August 13-17 and Mackay from August 22-26, the start of a gruelling 12 months featuring 20 Test matches.

Weatherald will resume his opening batting partnership with Travis Head after playing all five Tests last summer against England.

The Darwin-born left-hander made only 201 runs at an average of 22.33 but has been given another chance to enhance his Test credentials.

AAP

World.title: NSW gold-antimony plant springs to life as Larvotto nears production
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears NSW gold-antimony plant springs to life as Larvotto nears production Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright July 21, 2026 — 12:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In a red-letter milestone for the company, Larvotto Resources has kicked off staged commissioning at its Hillgrove antimony-gold mine in New South Wales, marking the next step in a carefully sequenced restart that began underground at its nearby Metz mine. Larvotto’s underground contractor PYBAR has been pushing forward with the Metz workings and rehabilitating old drives since mining restarted, with first development ore delivered to surface stockpiles in May and ore stockpiles continuing to build since then. Larvotto Resources’ secondary crusher with the fine ore storage behind, at the company’s Hillgrove antimony-gold operation in NSW. That ore has now begun moving from stockpiles to the run-of-mine pad, before being fed into the primary jaw crusher, closed-circuit secondary crusher and screening circuit. From there, the material is then conveyed to the fine ore bin. The company says the crushing, screening and fine ore storage section has been successfully commissioned as the first stage of the plant restart. The resulting ore is now sitting in storage ready to feed the milling circuit during the upcoming phase of wet-end commissioning.



‘Hillgrove will become Australia’s largest antimony producer, and with tungsten potential growing.’ Larvotto Resources managing director Ron Heeks Once the fine ore bin is full, Larvotto plans to run the crushing circuit on waste for a limited period to generate crushed rock for various engineering requirements, allowing more time to bed the crushing system down. It will also give operators familiarisation time on the circuit. EPCM contractor Interquip, meanwhile, is completing its work on the communications, electrical, instrumentation and control systems at the wet end of the plant before that phase is commissioned. Hillgrove is forecast to become Australia’s second and largest producing antimony mine, with Larvotto pointing to the planned production of around 4900 tonnes of antimony -almost seven per cent of global production - and more than 40,000 ounces of gold a year across the current seven-year mine life. The company says its tungsten testwork is continuing, with multiple zones of tungsten mineralisation identified and unrecovered tungsten from previous operations sitting in the old tailings dam, all pointing to the potential for a third critical minerals string to Hillgrove’s bow.



Larvotto Resources managing director Ron Heeks said: “The commencement of commissioning is a defining milestone for Larvotto and reflects the significant progress made over the past twelve months since the plant refurbishment started. To reach this point is a tremendous achievement by our operations team and Interquip, the build contractors, and demonstrates the quality of execution, especially given the unique challenges that were, and continue to be, created by the Hormuz conflict on equipment deliveries.” Larvotto’s marketing pathways are also falling into place. Last month, the company locked in a binding seven-year offtake deal with Glencore International for its Hillgrove gold concentrate, complementing its previously announced antimony concentrate agreement with Wogen Resources. The Glencore agreement is expected to cover 15,000 dry metric tonnes of gold concentrate a year. Larvotto is also pushing ahead with its Modification 5 application process with the NSW government, seeking approval to lift its processing capacity from 250,000 to 500,000 tonnes a year, while also enabling dry-stack tailings and other environmental improvements. The company says responses to questions from the NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure and other stakeholders are being finalised and are expected to be submitted by the end of July. Larvotto does not view the matters raised as material issues, instead describing them as being part of the appropriate level of review expected for a project of Hillgrove’s scale and strategic importance. With ore already passing through the front end of the plant, offtake partners signed up for its key concentrate products and the early stages of its process plant commissioning underway, Hillgrove is steadily working through its transition from development to a producing mine.



For Larvotto, the next few weeks will be all about transforming a historic mining field into a modern critical minerals operation, with antimony and gold leading the production charge and the prospect of a valuable tungsten by-product adding another layer of upside. World.title: No preference deal yet, but Hanson vows to put Labor last in Secret Harbour byelection
World.content:
NationalWAOne Nation No preference deal yet, but Hanson vows to put Labor last in Secret Harbour byelection Michael Philipps July 21, 2026 — 12:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson says a preference deal is yet to be struck with WA’s Liberal party ahead of the upcoming Secret Harbour byelection, but vowed to put both the Greens and Labor last. Speaking after her appearance at a business breakfast hosted by The West Australian, the federal senator said she hoped to work with the Liberals and Nationals to take the seat from Labor. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson campaigning with candidate Luke Herdegen in Secret Harbour on Monday. “This will be a test case, the same as when we won seven seats in the South Australian parliament,” Hanson said. “A deal has not been struck, but we will be putting Labor last and the Greens second last.”



The Queensland senator also dubbed Gina Rinehart “a wonderful West Australian” while defending the billionaire mining heiress’ support for One Nation. Hanson has received criticism from opposing political parties and the media after Rinehart provided significant support for the Queenslander, including an airplane, and as photos emerged of the pair holidaying in Europe. “Look at those taxes, royalties, and jobs that she provides the state,” Hanson told the audience after the Hancock Prospecting boss was brought up by West Australian editor Chris Dore at the breakfast event. “It didn’t cost the taxpayer one cent for my trip overseas. Not one cent.



“You think that she’s come with a silver spoon. She didn’t. “She had to borrow everything and was flat out in the very start to pay the bills. She’s built up that company. “A very smart, clever woman. And even now, to this day, who supports the [Royal] Flying Doctor Service. Who supports the Olympic swimmers and the lobbyists. “She’s a very proud, patriotic Australian, and she sees the same in me.” Hanson also used her appearance to highlight the important role WA played in the nation’s economy while also addressing the continued housing crisis in the state.



She said WA was being held back by the federal government. Related Article Political leadership Why these Brisbane Islamic school students spoke to Pauline Hanson “Western Australia helps to pay this nation’s bills. Your royalties fund the services here,” she said. “Your taxes fund them everywhere else. Western Australia is home to roughly one in nine Australians, but generates one in $6 of national economic output. “Western Australia generates almost one in $5 of national business investment. It generates almost half of the country’s exported goods.



“But your businesses are being held back by this government.” Hanson pointed to Perth’s rental vacancy rate of 0.6 per cent – the tightest capital city in the country after Darwin – and blamed the federal government’s migration policy for the increase. “Families with nowhere to live in the richest state in the nation. And let me tell you why there’s nowhere to live, it’s not a mystery,” she said. “Last year, this country’s population grew by more than 400,000 people. In the same year, we finished about 173,000 homes, nearly 2½ people for every new home, and it’s not slowing down. “In just four years, this government will have added almost 1.6 million people through net overseas migration. Nearly one million arrived in 2022 and 2023 alone.



“This government is running the biggest migration program in our history, and building nowhere near the homes to match it. Then it acts surprised when your kids can’t afford a house and services are overwhelmed. “That’s not compassion. That’s negligence.” More to come.

World.title: Double blow for Rabbitohs after Murray, Mitchell injury prognoses revealed
World.content:
South Sydney superstar Latrell Mitchell may not play again this year, in a second blow to the Rabbitohs’ finals chances after captain Cameron Murray succumbed to an ankle injury.

Murray suffered the injury in the loss to Canberra on Saturday night and is expected to be sidelined for up to a month. The loss of the NSW forward is set to be compounded by the news that Mitchell is struggling to return to the field due to his own injury issues.

Cameron Murray and Latrell Mitchell, Souths’ highest-paid players, are due for more time on the sidelines.

Mitchell’s scheduled return from a back injury last month was aborted after he tore his calf in training. It was hoped Mitchell could be fit for the round-23 clash against Parramatta on August 8, but there is no guarantee he will play again this year.

The loss of the star duo is a huge blow for the Rabbitohs, who are in seventh position on the ladder and fighting for one of the final spots in the top eight.

World.title: Manhattan jags 20g/t gold at new undrilled Canadian prospect
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Manhattan jags 20g/t gold at new undrilled Canadian prospect Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward July 21, 2026 — 12:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Manhattan Gold Corporation has unearthed a swag of high-grade gold results from first-pass sampling at its newly acquired and never-before-drilled Vanquish prospect in Nunavut, Canada, hitting a hefty 20 grams per tonne (g/t) gold in testing. The results from a quickfire channel and grab sampling program at the prospect within the company’s expansive Hook Lake project included impressive channel assays of 18.55g/t gold over 0.3 metres and 15.45g/t gold over 0.4m. Manhattan Gold’s Hook Lake project area in Nunavut, Canada. The new work at Vanquish, which sits 80 kilometres west of Manhattan’s flagship Jaws target, has now identified gold mineralisation over at least 131 metres of strike, significantly expanding a footprint previously defined by historic surface trenching that returned 5.75g/t gold over 1.5m. Manhattan only recently acquired the prospect in April after a review of historic data identified the biggest gold-arsenic till anomaly within the Kaminak greenstone belt, which forms part of the broader Rankin Ennadai greenstone belt.



‘Drilling at Jaws is advancing,samples from the initial holes are being analysed and first assay results are expected shortly.’ Manhattan Gold Corporation tecnical advisor Eric Sondergaard Despite the compelling geochemical smoke, the target has never been kissed by the drill bit. The company says the reconnaissance sampling at Vanquish was completed during the mobilisation of the drill rig and supporting equipment to Jaws. Vanquish is one of 12 prospects within Manhattan’s 665-square-kilometre Hook Lake project, which sits in the underexplored but highly prospective Rankin-Ennadai greenstone belt. The belt is also home to mining giant Agnico Eagle’s 6.7-million-ounce Meliadine operation, 225 kilometres to the northeast and one of Canada’s largest gold mines. The company says this underlines the world-class gold endowment of the region and suggests it has the potential for further significant deposits. Manhattan Gold Corporation technical advisor Eric Sondergaard said: “The early results from Vanquish are particularly exciting. This is a newly acquired, never- drilled prospect where a limited first-pass program has already delivered grades of up to 20g/t gold and confirmed mineralisation across 131 metres of strike.”



Manhattan’s current work is focused on a maiden reverse circulation program at its flagship Jaws target, where drilling in the 1980’s outlined a historical foreign resource estimate of 3.4 million tonnes grading 2.38g/t gold for a contained 285,000 ounces. The company is quick to say that the estimate is not compliant with the modern JORC code and it is now eagerly awaiting the first batch of assays from its Jaws drilling program to firm up the numbers for conversion into a JORC-compliant inventory. First results are expected in the coming weeks. Beyond Jaws and Vanquish, the Hook Lake project hosts a grab-bag of other compelling targets. These include the never-drilled Quantum and Lotus prospects, which have returned surface gold samples of 16.75g/t and 8.01g/t respectively. Manhattan’s other key target is Spectre, a high-grade polymetallic Volcanogenic Massive Sulphide (VMS) system where drilling in the 1970’s hit a mouthwatering 10.51m at 2.91 per cent copper, 6.7 per cent zinc and 95.67g/t silver. The company plans to integrate the new high-grade gold results with recently acquired magnetic and LiDAR data to refine the structural model and prioritise drill targets at Vanquish.



With the drill rods turning at its flagship Jaws prospect and a brand new, high-grade discovery at Vanquish screaming to be tested, Manhattan appears to be systematically building a serious inventory of gold targets. Punters will likely be watching to see if the drill bit at Jaws can deliver what the surface rocks at Vanquish are already suggesting. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? World.title: Every phone in Australia will get the same text on Monday. That’s if it works
World.content:
PoliticsFederalEmergency services Every phone in Australia will get the same text on Monday. That’s if it works Mike Foley July 21, 2026 — 12:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Years of planning have gone into the 10-second alarm that will sound on up to 25 million phones around Australia on Monday, July 27, but officials will be holding their breath in case of unpredictable mishaps for the AusAlert test. The new national warning system will use the same broadcast technology that operates in more than 30 countries, many of which found gremlins in the system during their testing over the past decade. Loading New Zealanders were awoken in the middle of the night, Germans were bemused when the message did not arrive and surprised when it sounded 20 minutes late, Welsh speakers saw a spelling error in the alert’s text and millions of UK and Canadian residents missed out altogether. Australia’s test is scheduled to sound at 2pm on Monday July 27, with a text message that reads: “This is a TEST alert of AusAlert, Australia’s new emergency warning system. NO ACTION IS REQUIRED.”



Fingers and toes will be crossed that is what happens. But mistakes may be inevitable and are, in fact, needed to iron out the kinks in such a big system, says Queensland University of Technology associate professor Paula Dootson. “There’s teething problems with any new technology. There’ll be technical challenges, there’ll be operational challenges, we will see it all,” said Dootson, who studies emergency communications. Emergency Management Minister Kristy McBain said the national test was intended to iron out any issues. Dominic Lorrimer “We will figure out where the black spots are, and what phones we can’t reach people on, if they’re on older models, as well as language accessibility.” The new national alert system will be used to issue a wide range of warnings, including for natural disasters, threats to public safety such as shooting incidents, as well as health and biosecurity threats like a disease outbreak.



Experts have said that victim-survivors of domestic violence and others who rely on secret or hidden phones could be endangered by the alert. If you do not wish the phone to sound, it should be switched off at least one hour before the test and remain off for at least one hour after. There is no plan to immediately replace existing state-run warning systems, including for natural disasters, which will continue to operate in tandem with AusAlert over the high-risk summer period. AusAlert uses cell broadcast technology not the SMS relied on by states to issue warnings. Cell broadcast sends messages from selected mobile phone towers to every compatible device within that towers’ range. By selecting which towers transmit, the message can be targeted to people who need to see it, often down to a street-by-street level of accuracy.



Targeted messages can boost people’s confidence in emergency warnings, Dootson said. Related Article Updated

Emergency services Hear the shrill new emergency alert coming to every mobile in Australia “If people are alerted to a flood that is nowhere near them, that can create distrust in the efficacy of the system. The closer you can get, the more relevant you can make the message, the more people will trust it and actually take action.” Cell broadcast does not need phone numbers to reach a device, and it is not subject to network congestion that affects SMS. With cell broadcast alerts, all phones entering the broadcast area will receive the message for however long the alert remains active. Dootson said it was important to dispel misconceptions about privacy concerns with cell broadcast technology.



“It just sends a ping out to a device in a geographic fenced area to say there’s a threat. A lot of people think that they’re identified as an individual. That’s absolutely not what’s happening.” Emergency Management Minister Kristy McBain said the national test was intended to iron out any issues. A relatively small number of people with older model phones may not receive the message, she said. Targeted messages can boost people’s confidence in emergency warnings, Dootson said. NSW Police “The purpose of testing is to find and fix issues now, so AusAlert is ready to help keep Australians safe during real emergencies,” she said. “Some people may not receive the alert if their device is not compatible, does not have the latest software, is switched off, in aeroplane mode, is outside mobile coverage, or not connected to a mobile tower at the time.”



Testing troubles When Germany tested its cell broadcast warning system in December 2022, the message scheduled to be sent in the morning arrived 20 minutes late to many phones. An “all clear” follow-up message scheduled for later in the day also failed to broadcast to many phones. Later tests in 2023 and 2025 revealed issues with certain phones screening out the alert due to user settings, despite the system being designed to notify all phones. Related Article Domestic violence Emergency alert test may expose DV victims’ safe phones In the UK in April 2023, up to 10 million phones missed out on the national emergency test message, among other issues for some who did not receive the message if they were only connected to a Wi-Fi network. In Canada in May 2018, a coding error prevented the national test being sent to millions of residents in Quebec.



Many New Zealanders woke in fright in the early hours of October 3, 2017 when cell broadcast technology accidentally sent its message at 1.30am, with the government agency responsible blaming the rude timing on its European technology contractor. Despite the growing global uptake of cell broadcast systems, Dootson expects it will compliment rather than replace existing systems. “Landlines will be here forever, radio will be here forever. There’ll always be scenarios where things go wrong, power goes out, systems go down. We need as much redundancy in our communication processes as possible. “We know people go to the authority for the trusted information, we know they make sense of that information with their community groups on social media, and we know some people just prefer to pick up the phone, so adding one extra channel will not mean getting rid of anything else.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Shallow gold hits put Pacgold on fast track to SA mine restart
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Shallow gold hits put Pacgold on fast track to SA mine restart Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Penny Taylor July 21, 2026 — 12:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Pacgold has unearthed significant shallow oxide gold on the edge of the historical Vertigo open pit at its wholly owned White Dam project in South Australia, potentially putting the mine’s restart on the fast track. The recently completed reverse circulation drilling began with an initial 178-hole campaign before a successful first phase prompted a further 102-hole infill and extension program. The latest round was designed to upgrade much of Vertigo’s inferred resource into the higher-confidence indicated category, strengthening pit design, reserve estimation and mine planning. Aerial view showing the Vertigo deposit (bottom left), the Hannaford pit and existing heap-leach pad (upper centre), and the operating plant and SART facility (upper right) at Pacgold’s White Dam gold project in South Australia. The program delivered some impressive shallow hits, with highlights including 4 metres grading 3.1 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from surface, including a 1m slice grading 7.2g/t gold. Other notable results delivered 6m grading 2.2g/t gold from surface, 11m grading 1.2g/t gold also from surface, 17m grading 0.9g/t gold from 6m and 13m grading 1.3g/t gold from a depth of 14m.



‘The development from ore discovered north and east of the pit will drastically reduce pre-strip costs and bring forward gold production.’ Pacgold managing director Matthew Boyes Beyond the headline intersections, the final assays also confirmed shallow northern and western extensions to the Vertigo deposit outside the existing resource model, pointing to further resource growth. The results will now be incorporated into an updated resource estimate for Vertigo, currently being prepared by external consultants and slated for delivery early in the September quarter. Prior to the update, the White Dam project hosted a global resource of 4.6 million tonnes grading 0.7g/t gold for 102,000 ounces across the Vertigo, Hannaford and White Dam North deposits. Vertigo is the first of White Dam’s four deposits targeted for restart, putting it at the front of the queue to bring White Dam back into production. Management believes the shallow oxide mineralisation will improve both the economics and timing of bringing Vertigo back into production.



Pacgold managing director Matthew Boyes said: “These excellent shallow oxide intervals represent a very material win for Pacgold in respect to fast-tracking the restart of the Vertigo mine and getting shallow low-cost oxide dirt onto the old pad while extending the ore leaching capacity with the new pad expansion.” The company is already pushing forward with a heap-leach pad expansion, with engineering nearing completion ahead of construction tenders. The bigger plant will allow for additional oxide ore to be processed as operations ramp up. Since the mineralisation is shallow, oxidised and beside an existing pit, Pacgold believes it’s ideally suited for low-cost heap-leach processing, where a cyanide solution recovers gold without the expense of conventional milling. That winning combination could slash pre-strip waste removal, reduce working capital and bring forward the first new ounces of gold. Management says the focus will shortly shift to pit optimisation, mine design and cashflow modelling once the new resource model is complete. The rig has now moved on from Vertigo, with drilling already underway at White Dam North ahead of a spell at the nearby Rolling and Hannaford deposits. All three are expected to provide additional resource growth and future ore sources for the planned restart. The company is also preparing regional exploration drilling at the Wadnaminga, Wilkins, Green and Gold and Mary Mine prospects later this quarter as it hunts for additional ore sources within easy trucking distance of White Dam.



For a brownfield restart project such as White Dam, the gold’s proximity to the plant matters far more than the grades returned. Between 2010 and 2018, White Dam produced 180,000 ounces. It already has established open pits, a heap-leach facility, a processing plant and all the supporting infrastructure a new miner could want. Much of the operation was paid for by previous owners, allowing Pacgold to bring the project back into production far faster and cheaper than building a mine from scratch. The company’s efforts to restart mining in South Australia seem well-timed. While gold prices may have pulled back to US$4000 (A$5700) per ounce from their historic highs of more than US$5500 (A$7800) per ounce earlier in the year, major institutions remain bullish. J.P. Morgan has forecast a rebound to an average of A$6,000 per ounce in the final quarter of this year. Finding a source of low-cost, quick-to-mine ore could leave White Dam well placed if bullion regains momentum later this year. Against that backdrop, the White Dam story isn’t about chasing the next big discovery. It’s about systematically unlocking more ounces from an established mining operation and turning yesterday’s infrastructure into tomorrow’s cash flow. The latest drilling has strengthened the investment case for Vertigo to become the first White Dam deposit back in production, while longer term, Pacgold sees White Dam evolving into a regional processing hub. The next catalyst will be the updated resource model and mine plan, which could provide the blueprint for breathing new life into one of South Australia’s proven gold-producing operations. World.title: Jobs to go at Nine’s metro mastheads in restructure to drive digital push
World.content:
Breaking BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing Jobs to go at Nine’s metro mastheads in restructure to drive digital push Calum Jaspan July 21, 2026 — 12:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nine’s publishing division, which includes this masthead, will make dozens of roles redundant as part of a restructure to sharpen its focus on digital news amid a tough advertising market and rapid technological disruption in the media industry. About 30 voluntary redundancies will be initially offered to staff at The Sydney Morning Herald, The Age, WAToday and Brisbane Times as the division pushes for more digital subscribers, with staff in the division’s print operations team and free news site nine.com.au also facing cuts. Nine is announcing job cuts at The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age. Paul Rovere Managing director of the publishing division Tory Maguire informed staff of the upcoming changes in an email and town hall meeting on Tuesday morning, saying that the business needed to adapt to a changing media landscape to protect its journalism. This includes investing in new areas to connect with new audiences, she said. “In particular we need to keep shifting towards the digital-first future,” Maguire said, though she added that print revenue has held up better than previously expected.



Maguire said the company would engage with the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance (MEAA) union that represents journalists. Related Article Exclusive

Media & marketing Up to 200 staff to go as Seven’s owner swings the axe Nine signed a landmark deal with Microsoft earlier this month, meaning the tech giant’s AI chatbot Copilot will reference content from the company’s mastheads in its search results, with the media company compensated in return. A briefing from investment bank UBS this month said revenue impact from the Microsoft deal would not have a major impact on the company’s bottom line, suggesting it is worth less than $25 million, but said it was “positive for future potential deals” ahead of expected legislation to bring tech giants to the bargaining table. News organisations around the world are adapting to the rapid uptake of AI chatbots as a tool for consuming information. Google, for example, has rolled out its AI Overview function over the past two years at the top of its search results, leading to a decline in click-through traffic both to news websites and all other web domains. Media union representative Cassie Derrick said the cuts were devastating and called on Nine to give more information about the cuts to the MEAA.



“Nine must engage in genuine consultation with staff through their union, and do everything possible to avoid forced redundancies, including redeployment and voluntary options,” Derrick said. “Newsrooms cannot keep absorbing job cuts without consequences for workloads, diversity, quality journalism and the ability of journalists to hold power to account.” The Australian Financial Review will not be affected by the cuts. Publishing was Nine’s second best-performing division in its 2025 full-year results, with revenue of $526 million and earnings, before a common range of deductions, of $153 million. Declines to print sales were offset by subscriber growth, the company said in its annual report last year. Projections show the division’s earnings are expected to be flat in the upcoming 2026 results, delivered in August. The company took $33 million in costs out of the division in the 2025 financial year. Nine has since sold its share of digital real estate business Domain for $1.4 billion, as well as its talkback radio division. It also purchased outdoor media company QMS for $850 million. World.title: NSW gold-antimony plant springs to life as Larvotto nears production
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears NSW gold-antimony plant springs to life as Larvotto nears production Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright July 21, 2026 — 12:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In a red-letter milestone for the company, Larvotto Resources has kicked off staged commissioning at its Hillgrove antimony-gold mine in New South Wales, marking the next step in a carefully sequenced restart that began underground at its nearby Metz mine. Larvotto’s underground contractor PYBAR has been pushing forward with the Metz workings and rehabilitating old drives since mining restarted, with first development ore delivered to surface stockpiles in May and ore stockpiles continuing to build since then. Larvotto Resources’ secondary crusher with the fine ore storage behind, at the company’s Hillgrove antimony-gold operation in NSW. That ore has now begun moving from stockpiles to the run-of-mine pad, before being fed into the primary jaw crusher, closed-circuit secondary crusher and screening circuit. From there, the material is then conveyed to the fine ore bin. The company says the crushing, screening and fine ore storage section has been successfully commissioned as the first stage of the plant restart. The resulting ore is now sitting in storage ready to feed the milling circuit during the upcoming phase of wet-end commissioning.



‘Hillgrove will become Australia’s largest antimony producer, and with tungsten potential growing.’ Larvotto Resources managing director Ron Heeks Once the fine ore bin is full, Larvotto plans to run the crushing circuit on waste for a limited period to generate crushed rock for various engineering requirements, allowing more time to bed the crushing system down. It will also give operators familiarisation time on the circuit. EPCM contractor Interquip, meanwhile, is completing its work on the communications, electrical, instrumentation and control systems at the wet end of the plant before that phase is commissioned. Hillgrove is forecast to become Australia’s second and largest producing antimony mine, with Larvotto pointing to the planned production of around 4900 tonnes of antimony -almost seven per cent of global production - and more than 40,000 ounces of gold a year across the current seven-year mine life. The company says its tungsten testwork is continuing, with multiple zones of tungsten mineralisation identified and unrecovered tungsten from previous operations sitting in the old tailings dam, all pointing to the potential for a third critical minerals string to Hillgrove’s bow.



Larvotto Resources managing director Ron Heeks said: “The commencement of commissioning is a defining milestone for Larvotto and reflects the significant progress made over the past twelve months since the plant refurbishment started. To reach this point is a tremendous achievement by our operations team and Interquip, the build contractors, and demonstrates the quality of execution, especially given the unique challenges that were, and continue to be, created by the Hormuz conflict on equipment deliveries.” Larvotto’s marketing pathways are also falling into place. Last month, the company locked in a binding seven-year offtake deal with Glencore International for its Hillgrove gold concentrate, complementing its previously announced antimony concentrate agreement with Wogen Resources. The Glencore agreement is expected to cover 15,000 dry metric tonnes of gold concentrate a year. Larvotto is also pushing ahead with its Modification 5 application process with the NSW government, seeking approval to lift its processing capacity from 250,000 to 500,000 tonnes a year, while also enabling dry-stack tailings and other environmental improvements. The company says responses to questions from the NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure and other stakeholders are being finalised and are expected to be submitted by the end of July. Larvotto does not view the matters raised as material issues, instead describing them as being part of the appropriate level of review expected for a project of Hillgrove’s scale and strategic importance. With ore already passing through the front end of the plant, offtake partners signed up for its key concentrate products and the early stages of its process plant commissioning underway, Hillgrove is steadily working through its transition from development to a producing mine.



For Larvotto, the next few weeks will be all about transforming a historic mining field into a modern critical minerals operation, with antimony and gold leading the production charge and the prospect of a valuable tungsten by-product adding another layer of upside. World.title: Double blow for Rabbitohs after Murray, Mitchell injury prognoses revealed
World.content:
South Sydney superstar Latrell Mitchell may not play again this year, in a second blow to the Rabbitohs’ finals chances after captain Cameron Murray succumbed to an ankle injury.

Murray suffered the injury in the loss to Canberra on Saturday night and is expected to be sidelined for up to a month. The loss of the NSW forward is set to be compounded by the news that Mitchell is struggling to return to the field due to his own injury issues.

Cameron Murray and Latrell Mitchell, Souths’ highest-paid players, are due for more time on the sidelines.

Mitchell’s scheduled return from a back injury last month was aborted after he tore his calf in training. It was hoped Mitchell could be fit for the round-23 clash against Parramatta on August 8, but there is no guarantee he will play again this year.

The loss of the star duo is a huge blow for the Rabbitohs, who are in seventh position on the ladder and fighting for one of the final spots in the top eight.

World.title: Manhattan jags 20g/t gold at new undrilled Canadian prospect
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Manhattan jags 20g/t gold at new undrilled Canadian prospect Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward July 21, 2026 — 12:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Manhattan Gold Corporation has unearthed a swag of high-grade gold results from first-pass sampling at its newly acquired and never-before-drilled Vanquish prospect in Nunavut, Canada, hitting a hefty 20 grams per tonne (g/t) gold in testing. The results from a quickfire channel and grab sampling program at the prospect within the company’s expansive Hook Lake project included impressive channel assays of 18.55g/t gold over 0.3 metres and 15.45g/t gold over 0.4m. Manhattan Gold’s Hook Lake project area in Nunavut, Canada. The new work at Vanquish, which sits 80 kilometres west of Manhattan’s flagship Jaws target, has now identified gold mineralisation over at least 131 metres of strike, significantly expanding a footprint previously defined by historic surface trenching that returned 5.75g/t gold over 1.5m. Manhattan only recently acquired the prospect in April after a review of historic data identified the biggest gold-arsenic till anomaly within the Kaminak greenstone belt, which forms part of the broader Rankin Ennadai greenstone belt.



‘Drilling at Jaws is advancing,samples from the initial holes are being analysed and first assay results are expected shortly.’ Manhattan Gold Corporation tecnical advisor Eric Sondergaard Despite the compelling geochemical smoke, the target has never been kissed by the drill bit. The company says the reconnaissance sampling at Vanquish was completed during the mobilisation of the drill rig and supporting equipment to Jaws. Vanquish is one of 12 prospects within Manhattan’s 665-square-kilometre Hook Lake project, which sits in the underexplored but highly prospective Rankin-Ennadai greenstone belt. The belt is also home to mining giant Agnico Eagle’s 6.7-million-ounce Meliadine operation, 225 kilometres to the northeast and one of Canada’s largest gold mines. The company says this underlines the world-class gold endowment of the region and suggests it has the potential for further significant deposits. Manhattan Gold Corporation technical advisor Eric Sondergaard said: “The early results from Vanquish are particularly exciting. This is a newly acquired, never- drilled prospect where a limited first-pass program has already delivered grades of up to 20g/t gold and confirmed mineralisation across 131 metres of strike.”



Manhattan’s current work is focused on a maiden reverse circulation program at its flagship Jaws target, where drilling in the 1980’s outlined a historical foreign resource estimate of 3.4 million tonnes grading 2.38g/t gold for a contained 285,000 ounces. The company is quick to say that the estimate is not compliant with the modern JORC code and it is now eagerly awaiting the first batch of assays from its Jaws drilling program to firm up the numbers for conversion into a JORC-compliant inventory. First results are expected in the coming weeks. Beyond Jaws and Vanquish, the Hook Lake project hosts a grab-bag of other compelling targets. These include the never-drilled Quantum and Lotus prospects, which have returned surface gold samples of 16.75g/t and 8.01g/t respectively. Manhattan’s other key target is Spectre, a high-grade polymetallic Volcanogenic Massive Sulphide (VMS) system where drilling in the 1970’s hit a mouthwatering 10.51m at 2.91 per cent copper, 6.7 per cent zinc and 95.67g/t silver. The company plans to integrate the new high-grade gold results with recently acquired magnetic and LiDAR data to refine the structural model and prioritise drill targets at Vanquish.



With the drill rods turning at its flagship Jaws prospect and a brand new, high-grade discovery at Vanquish screaming to be tested, Manhattan appears to be systematically building a serious inventory of gold targets. Punters will likely be watching to see if the drill bit at Jaws can deliver what the surface rocks at Vanquish are already suggesting. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting?
